records.p: The pointed crest, densely barred pale-brown underside and broad, paddle-shaped wings distinguish this baza in flight (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Jerdon’s Baza is recorded from Mindanao, including the Zamboanga Peninsula and Davao Oriental, and from Southern Leyte. Western Mindanao observations include historical reports from the Zamboanga area (Lint & Stott, 1948; GIZ, 2013; GBIF.org, 2026). The Jerdon's Baza is reported from forests, rivers and streams, as well as grasslands and other open areas. Birds wintering in Southeast Asia sometimes gather in small groups; prey is taken during short sallies from a concealed perch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

records.p: A grayish face, white throat with a median dark line, and barred rufous-and-white abdomen distinguish adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Grey-faced Buzzard has been recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol and Siargao. On Mindanao, its localities include the Mount Kitanglad Range and Cinchona Forest Reserve in Bukidnon, Mount Tagubud in Davao de Oro, Mount Melibengoy in South Cotabato, and the Pasonanca area of the Zamboanga Peninsula. Bohol records include the Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Grey-faced Buzzard is reported from forests. McGregor reported substantial migration flocks passing the Calayan and Batan islands, with birds gathering in large numbers (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adult male Pied Harriers have black heads and breasts, white bellies and rumps, and contrasting silvery wing panels (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.; McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pied Harrier has been reported from Mindanao, Bohol and Leyte, including the Bukidnon and Lake Lanao areas of Mindanao. Historical field observations also documented the species on Mindanao and Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Lint & Stott, 1948). The species searches open terrain in low, buoyant flight, alternating flaps and glides (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pied Harrier is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, as well as agricultural land.

records.p: Adults are pale grey above and white below, with dark shoulder patches and reddish eyes (BirdLife South Africa, n.d.). The Black-winged Kite has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). Hovering while searching for prey is a characteristic hunting behavior (BirdLife South Africa, n.d.). The Black-winged Kite is reported from grasslands and other open areas, shrublands, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats.

records.p: Adults show dark upperparts, a pale throat and upper breast, and chestnut-rufous belly and underwing-coverts; juveniles are paler below (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Rufous-bellied Eagle has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rufous-bellied Eagle is reported from forests. The Rufous-bellied Eagle hunts by diving from height or waiting on a perch before striking prey (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Compared with the Crested Honey Buzzard, this Philippine honey-buzzard has shorter wings and a shorter, more square-ended tail. The wing edges are relatively parallel in flight, giving this species a compact, shorter-winged outline compared with P. ptilorhynchus. Its resemblance to the Philippine Hawk-Eagle can complicate distant identification (Gamauf et al., 1998). The Philippine Honey Buzzard is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Honey Buzzard is reported from forests. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 20.9 mm, Kipp’s distance of 113.2 mm, and wing length of 378.5 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 29.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: In flight, the Philippine Eagle shows a long tail and rounded wings (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, n.d.). The Philippine Eagle has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. Its Mindanao records include the Mount Apo, Busa, Hamiguitan, Pasian and Melibengoy regions. A historical sighting was also reported from the Zamboanga area, without establishing current occupancy there (Lint & Stott, 1948; GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Luczon et al., 2014). On Mindanao, Philippine Eagles nest in large trees within lowland dipterocarp and upper hill forest, and some nests occur near the transition to montane or mossy forest. Studied nest trees often stood on steep slopes and ravines (Philippine Eagle Foundation, n.d.). Tracking of six adults found varied use of forest vegetation around nesting areas (Sutton et al., 2024). A nesting study at Mount Sinaka documented a diet that included civets and Philippine colugos (Ibañez et al., 2003). An eastern Mindanao habitat model also found overlap between predicted nesting habitat and areas designated for mining or ancestral domains (Sutton et al., 2026; University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, n.d.). A genomic study compared 20 wild-captive and 15 captive-bred Philippine Eagles, finding higher genomic inbreeding among the wild-captive individuals sampled (Pascual et al., 2026). Analysis of 32 Philippine Eagles from the Greater Mindanao faunal region identified at least two maternal lineages and low mitochondrial nucleotide diversity (π = 0.00054 ± 0.00030) (Bacus et al., 2025). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: The adult male has a slaty upper body, chestnut-tinged breast, and a narrow dark median streak on the white throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Japanese Sparrowhawk has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary (GBIF.org, 2026). The Japanese Sparrowhawk is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats.

In flight, narrow pointed wings with only four primary fingers and little underwing-covert pattern distinguish it from other sparrowhawks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chinese Sparrowhawk is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Tagubud, and Davao de Oro. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chinese Sparrowhawk is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats. It breeds in northeastern Asia, then migrates through Southeast Asia to wintering areas including the Philippines (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Juveniles show bold dark tail bands and a yellow orbital ring; compared with Japanese Sparrowhawk they have a proportionately longer tail and rounder wings (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Besra has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, Mount Pasian, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Besra is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats. The species is resident or partly migratory over its Asian range; its movements vary among populations (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A white head with a dark line running through the eye accompanies long narrow wings and dark upperparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Osprey has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao del Norte. On Leyte, records include Lake Danao (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Osprey captures fish by plunging feet-first into water (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Osprey is reported from rivers and streams as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

The breeding male combines a brown head, white neck stripe, and very elongated pointed central tail feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Northern Pintail is recorded on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Northern Pintail is reported from freshwater wetlands. A Philippine observation recorded large flocks on Manila Bay during January and February, representing wintering-season behavior (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 59.9 mm, wing length of 268.2 mm, tail length of 87.2 mm, and body mass of 1156 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 20.9 mm, bill depth of 15.8 mm, and tarsus length of 39.8 mm for Anas zonorhyncha (Tobias et al., 2022). A historical spot-billed duck observation was reported from the Davao area of Mindanao under the former broad species name Anas poecilorhyncha. Its identification as the currently recognized Eastern Spot-billed Duck remains unresolved, and the report is treated as an exceptional occurrence (Hornskov, 1995; Birds of the World, n.d.). The Eastern Spot-billed Duck is reported from freshwater and coastal wetland habitats. The historical Davao report was made under a broader, pre-split name and does not establish regular local occurrence.

records.p: Adults have a dark-brown crown, a narrow black stripe along the back of the neck, a grey-mottled face and whitish throat. The rufous-brown upper breast and flanks bear conspicuous pale spots, and the undertail coverts are barred black and white (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Spotted Whistling-Duck has a historical record from the Zamboanga area of western Mindanao. Its regular occurrence in the region has not been established (Lint & Stott, 1948). The Spotted Whistling Duck is reported from forest and freshwater wetlands, with a historical record from coastal marsh near Zamboanga. That older observation does not establish regular present-day occurrence in Greater Mindanao. AVONET lists a culmen length of 43.7 mm, wing length of 206.6 mm, tail length of 58.6 mm, and body mass of 800 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 16.8 mm, bill depth of 14.1 mm, and tarsus length of 43.6 mm for Dendrocygna guttata (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 30.4 mm, Kipp’s distance of 55.6 mm, and wing length of 206.6 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 26.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: Breeding males have a buff crown, chestnut head, finely patterned gray body, and pale wing-coverts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Eurasian Wigeon is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Eurasian Wigeons graze on shoreline vegetation and also dabble for submerged aquatic plants (BirdLife International, 2017). The Eurasian Wigeon is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

Adult males are patterned grey with a black rear underside, whereas females are mottled brown with an orange-edged bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Gadwall is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Gadwall is reported from freshwater wetlands. The Gadwall feeds near the margins of freshwater bodies, keeping close to waterside vegetation (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Gadwalls feed mainly by dabbling in shallow water for aquatic vegetation, occasionally taking aquatic invertebrates (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d.).

r.short: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d.

records.p: Breeding males show a broad white supercilium and gray-blue forewing enclosing a green speculum (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Garganey has been documented on Mindanao, including Ligawasan Marsh (GBIF.org, 2026). The Garganey is reported from freshwater wetlands. The early seasonal description records males losing their conspicuous facial stripe in eclipse plumage (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Oberholser (1906) described the Luzon type as Collocalia unicolor amelis: a small swiftlet with dark sooty-brown upperparts, a somewhat darker head, a slightly paler rump, a gray-brown underside that is lightest on the throat, and entirely unfeathered tarsi. Unlike swiftlets with a conspicuous pale rump band, the rump was only subtly lighter than the back. His original comparisons were against species concepts and regional subspecies that have since changed, so these traits cannot by themselves exclude similar Philippine Aerodramus. In particular, the published Mt. Kitanglad review warns that many A. amelis and A. mearnsi observations cannot be separated reliably while birds are in flight. Voucher examination or other independently diagnostic evidence is needed for a confident record; historical specimens assigned outside the Philippines must be assessed under current taxonomy. The Ameline Swiftlet is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Ameline Swiftlet is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 7 mm, wing length of 113 mm, tail length of 48.9 mm, and body mass of 10.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 2.3 mm, bill depth of 2 mm, and tarsus length of 9.5 mm for Aerodramus fuciphagus (Tobias et al., 2022). The Edible-nest Swiftlet has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Edible-nest Swiftlet is reported from forests and settlements and disturbed habitats.

A small, predominantly dark swiftlet, approximately 10.5 cm long in a published field synopsis, with dark brown upperparts and rump, comparatively paler brown underparts and a shallowly forked tail. These features overlap with other Philippine Aerodramus and should not be treated as a conclusive visual diagnosis. A Mt. Kitanglad specimen-based review found that many large dark swiftlet sightings could not be confidently separated as A. mearnsi or A. amelis; its confirmed A. mearnsi evidence came from collected specimens. Examine vouchers, particularly tarsus feathering, tail form and bill proportions, before assigning ambiguous records to species (Peterson et al., 2008; BirdForum Opus). The Philippine Swiftlet has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Swiftlet is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats. AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 1.9 mm, Kipp’s distance of 74 mm and wing length of 109 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 67.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Mossy-nest Swiftlet is a small dark Aerodramus whose external appearance is too similar to other swiftlets for reliable identification from an ordinary flight sighting. In verified Southeast Asian breeding colonies, nests made with substantial moss and plant material provide an important contextual clue, although nests alone do not identify an unseen bird conclusively. A published Sarawak cave study documents the mossy-nest construction; that observation must not be presented as evidence of breeding in the Philippines. The existing Greater Mindanao account cites a single Philippine report from Basilan, not a documented local colony. Records should therefore rely on independently reviewed diagnostic photographs, a specimen or compelling documented breeding evidence rather than assigning every moss-lined cave nest or dark flying swiftlet to A. salangana. The Mossy-nest Swiftlet has a reported Philippine occurrence on Basilan, within the Greater Mindanao PAIC. The checklist describes this as a single record of the nominate subspecies; no comparable evidence was established here for a wider regional distribution, and the original specimen or observation merits further verification (Avibase, 2026). The Mossy-nest Swiftlet is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 6.7 mm, wing length of 113.5 mm, tail length of 50.5 mm, and body mass of 11.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 2.3 mm, bill depth of 2.1 mm, and tarsus length of 10.1 mm for Aerodramus salangana (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 2.2 mm, Kipp’s distance of 75.7 mm and wing length of 113.5 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 66.7 (Tobias et al., 2022).

An unusually large and dark swiftlet, with a markedly forked tail, uniform dark back and rump, and bare tarsi. Somadikarta (1967) explicitly used this combination to characterize Whitehead’s Swiftlet while reexamining historical assignments of other Pacific swiftlets; characters from birds subsequently separated from this species should not be transferred uncritically. A secondary field synopsis gives a length of approximately 14 cm, a relatively broad head and paler brown underparts, and describes the Mount Apo form origenis as darker overall. Because identification of Philippine swiftlets is difficult, the size and forked tail are clues rather than a substitute for examined voucher or other corroboration. The Whitehead's Swiftlet has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Mount Matutum, Mount Lumot, Misamis Oriental, and Sarangani (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). Nests attributed to the historical taxon on Luzon were built of green moss in a water-worn cave; eggs and nestlings were found in June (McGregor, 1909–1910). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 3 mm, Kipp’s distance of 94.1 mm, and wing length of 136 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 69.2 (Tobias et al., 2022).

Pale scaling on underparts and a white rump help distinguish it from Common Swift (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pacific Swift is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Tagubud, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Pacific Swift is reported from forests and settlements and disturbed habitats.

McGregor’s Oberholser’s Swiftlet was close to C. marginata in size and overall appearance but lacked white margins on the upper tail coverts and showed more extensive white on the abdomen. McGregor established these distinctions from examined historical specimens (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Ridgetop Swiftlet has records from Mindanao, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Ridgetop Swiftlet is listed from settled and disturbed landscapes in the regional working checklist, although specific nesting and roosting habitats are not documented by that classification.

records.p: In historical Philippine series, this small swiftlet had very dark green-glossed upperparts, conspicuous narrow white margins on the short upper tail coverts and a belly made largely white by broad pale feather edges. The dark undertail coverts were also narrowly edged with white. McGregor contrasted these white tail-covert margins with their absence in birds he treated as C. isonota (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Grey-rumped Swiftlet has records from Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Lake Danao. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Grey-rumped Swiftlet is reported from forests, caves and karst habitats. A historical breeding record on Sibuyan describes small rock-face colonies with hair-moss nests bound by saliva and two white eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Caves synthesis treated marginata as part of Collocalia esculenta and compared it with C. e. bagobo, reflecting the historical subspecies classification (Biodiversity Management Bureau, n.d.).

records.p: The Pygmy Swiftlet is especially small and has dark, glossy upperparts interrupted by a narrow white band across the rump. In McGregor’s Philippine specimens, the throat, breast and belly were mottled because pale feather tips contrasted with dusky bases and shaft streaks; the undertail coverts were dark. These characters are more informative than the historical account’s nesting descriptions, which require separate ecological verification (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pygmy Swiftlet is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Pygmy Swiftlet is reported from forests. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 1.6 mm, Kipp’s distance of 63.7 mm, and wing length of 92.8 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 68.6 (Tobias et al., 2022).

Small, uniformly grey-brown swift with narrow sickle-shaped wings and a long, deeply forked tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Palm Swift is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park and Davao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Asian Palm Swift captures small flying insects on the wing and is closely associated with fan palms (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Palm Swift is reported from grasslands and other open areas, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats.

A large, dark cigar-shaped swift with a squarish spiny tail and conspicuous white throat patch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-throated Needletail has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area, Mount Tagubud, Davao del Sur, and Davao de Oro (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-throated Needletail hunts flying insects on the wing, sometimes alongside other needletails, and has been recorded roosting in trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-throated Needletail is reported from forests as well as grasslands and other open areas.

A relatively large needletail with stiff projecting tail shafts, dark steel-blue to violet-glossed upperparts and conspicuous small pale patches on each side of the forehead. The original comparative treatment also described whitish areas on the sides of the lower body and undertail. Distant swifts may be difficult to assign without a clear view of these patterned regions (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Purple Needletail has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Purple Needletail is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 6.8 mm, Kipp’s distance of 151.6 mm and wing length of 213.7 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 70.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Philippine Spinetail is a short-tailed, dark swift with blue-black gloss across much of its body and a conspicuously white chin and throat. McGregor described white greater underwing coverts contrasting with darker surrounding feathers; these characters should be evaluated together because a brief distant view may show only a dark swift silhouette (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Spinetail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Spinetail is reported from forests. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 3 mm, Kipp’s distance of 115.6 mm, and wing length of 161.5 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 71.6 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A slim treeswift with glossy blue-black crown, long white eyebrow and malar streak; adult males have chestnut ear-coverts, females dark ear-coverts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Whiskered Treeswift is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Whiskered Treeswift captures small insects during short aerial sallies from an exposed perch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Whiskered Treeswift is reported from forests, grasslands and other open areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats.

Descriptions of adult males include a light head and underparts with darker upperparts and blue facial skin; females are predominantly dark with a pale-tipped tail (IUCN SSC Hornbill Specialist Group, 2020). Young birds can resemble the male but have smaller brown bills. The basilanicus form may lack the dark bill base seen in the typical form (IUCN SSC Hornbill Specialist Group, 2020). The Mindanao Hornbill has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Mindanao Hornbill inhabits primary and secondary rainforest, as well as forest edges, especially at lower elevations. It feeds mainly on fruit and seeds, occasionally taking animal food, and moves through the trees in pairs or small groups (IUCN SSC Hornbill Specialist Group, 2020; Gamalo et al., 2023). The cited account reports Mindanao and some adjacent smaller islands (IUCN SSC Hornbill Specialist Group, 2020). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: The male Samar Hornbill is similar in general plumage to the Mindanao Hornbill but has distinctly pale buff upper tail-coverts. Females resemble female Mindanao Hornbills more closely. McGregor highlighted the pale tail-coverts as a useful external identification character (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Samar Hornbill has been documented on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Samar Hornbill is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: The 60–65 cm male has a largely pale neck and upper breast, contrasting dark body and red bill/casque. Females are mainly dark with an orange-red bill and pouch. The cited range includes Mindanao and nearby islands (IUCN SSC Hornbill Specialist Group, n.d.). The Writhed Hornbill has been documented on Mindanao, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Lindasan, Mount Pasian, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Writhed Hornbill inhabits lowland rainforest and feeds mainly on fruit in the upper canopy. It moves between fruiting trees and roosts and occasionally catches insects in flight (IUCN SSC Hornbill Specialist Group, n.d.). Habitat loss and exploitation are reported threats (BirdLife International, 2020). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: This cryptically coloured nightjar has finely mottled grey, buff and dark-brown upperparts, pale marks along the scapulars and conspicuous light patches at the sides of the throat. In adult males described historically as Caprimulgus griseatus, broad white areas cross the outer primaries, the first reaching the shaft, and the outer tail feathers end in white. Adult females lack the broad terminal white tail patches and instead show barred, mottled outer tail feathers. McGregor’s key also grouped his C. mindanensis with griseatus on wing and tail characters, so those historical characters are not proof of identity within current Philippine nightjar species limits (McGregor, 1909). The Chirruping Nightjar is recorded on Mindanao, including Lanao del Sur and Misamis Oriental (Lepage, 2026). The Chirruping Nightjar is reported from grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. Whitehead collected two eggs near Cape Engaño, Luzon, on 26 May 1895, described as pale cream with faint lavender-gray and brown markings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The 2023 eBird taxonomy recognizes Chirruping Nightjar (Caprimulgus griseatus) as a separate species; older Philippine literature often used a broader nightjar classification (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2023).

r.full: Cornell Lab of Ornithology. (2023). 2023 eBird Taxonomy Update. https://science.ebird.org/use-ebird-data/the-ebird-taxonomy/2023-ebird-taxonomy-update

records.p: A mottled dark-brown nightjar; males show small white wing and tail patches, whereas females have reduced wing patches and lack the white outer tail marks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Gray Nightjar is recorded on Mindanao, including Lanao del Sur and Misamis Oriental (Lepage, 2026). The Grey Nightjar often roosts high on tree branches in daylight, unlike nightjars that regularly rest on the ground; feeds on insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Grey Nightjar is reported from forests, shrublands and agricultural areas.

The Philippine Nightjar has grey-brown cryptic plumage, a buff band behind the ear and two separate pale patches on the throat. Adult males have small white patches on the outer primaries and white toward the tips of the two outer tail-feather pairs. The white wing and tail markings are reduced or replaced by buff in females (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Nightjar is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). Early naturalists recorded hawking moths and beetles after sunset and resting in dense thickets by day (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Nightjar is reported from forests. AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 7.6 mm, Kipp’s distance of 82 mm and wing length of 170.2 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 48.2 (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Great Eared Nightjar complex is characterized by a large nightjar silhouette, conspicuous paired ear-like feather tufts and mottled brown upperparts with paler buff flecks. The sexes are similar in the broad characters listed by the source. Recent treatments split or propose splitting several island forms, including Philippine birds, so a feather-tuft diagnosis of the broader complex should not be mistaken for a comparison among all species-level taxa (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Great Eared Nightjar has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Lindasan, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Oriental. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Great Eared Nightjar is reported from forests, grasslands, other open habitats and shrublands. Whitehead reported birds leaving daytime cover near sunset and becoming active in the lower valleys of mountainous northern Luzon (McGregor, 1909–1910). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 7.1 mm, Kipp’s distance of 141 mm and wing length of 266.3 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 52.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

Breeding birds have a broken dark breast pattern, pale sandy upperparts, and a white forehead (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Kentish Plover is recorded on Mindanao, including Sarangani and Davao Oriental (Lepage, 2026). The Kentish Plover is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Siberian Sand Plover is relatively small and compact, with shorter legs and a less deeply based, less bulbous-tipped bill than the Greater Sand Plover. Breeding males show a broad cinnamon breast area with a narrow dark lower border and a strongly white forehead. Nonbreeding birds are difficult to distinguish from Tibetan Sand Plover; colder dark-brown upperparts, darker ear coverts, a stouter bill, and mottled flanks support, but do not independently establish, identification (Carey and Pang, 2024; updated 2025). A historical Lesser Sand Plover report from the Davao Gulf coast of Mindanao predates the separation of Siberian and Tibetan Sand Plovers. Its assignment to the present species Anarhynchus mongolus remains uncertain (Asian Development Bank, n.d.; Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2023). The Siberian Sand Plover is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. The 2023 eBird treatment separated Siberian Sand Plover (Anarhynchus mongolus) and Tibetan Sand Plover (A. atrifrons), formerly grouped under Lesser Sand Plover (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

r.full: Cornell Lab of Ornithology. (2023). 2023 eBird Taxonomy Update. https://science.ebird.org/use-ebird-data/the-ebird-taxonomy/2023-ebird-taxonomy-update

records.p: Adults show mottled upperwings, a white collar and rufous crown; breeding males carry a black forehead patch and black side patches on the breast (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Malaysian Plover is recorded on Mindanao, including Sarangani and Davao Oriental (Lepage, 2026). The Malaysian Plover occurs in pairs or small groups on sandy coastal habitats, including sparsely vegetated beaches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). A Singapore breeding study documented precocial chicks hiding among rocks and vegetation while adults maintained contact with quiet calls (Bird Society of Singapore, 2021). The Malaysian Plover is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

r.full: Bird Society of Singapore. (2021). Nesting Malaysian Plovers. Birds of Singapore. https://singaporebirds.com/blog/nesting-malaysian-plovers

records.p: A long-legged, upright plover with buff-brown plumage and yellowish-orange legs; breeding males show a rufous breast band bordered black below (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Oriental Plover is recorded from Davao Oriental, southeastern Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). The Oriental Plover is reported from grasslands and other open habitats, coastal and intertidal habitats. Northern breeders migrate toward northern Australia; records during passage in Southeast Asia are scarce (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The yellow orbital ring contrasts with a black face pattern in breeding adults (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Ringed Plover has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Ringed Plover is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats and freshwater wetlands.

Breeding birds show a black underside bordered by white and golden upperparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pacific Golden Plover is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Lituban–Quipit Watershed. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Pacific Golden Plover uses coastal mudflats as well as inland open grassy fields during migration and wintering (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pacific Golden Plover is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, agricultural areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

Long pointed wings, short red-based bill and a deeply forked tail distinguish the oriental pratincole (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Oriental Pratincole has records from Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include South Cotabato and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Pratincole captures flying insects over open terrain, often near freshwater, particularly in the early morning or evening (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Oriental Pratincole is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as grasslands and other open areas.

White wings with black tips identify this jacana in flight. Breeding adults have very long central tail feathers, unlike short-tailed nonbreeding birds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pheasant-tailed Jacana has records from Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Pheasant-tailed Jacana walks and forages over floating aquatic vegetation, occasionally feeding in open water (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Historical descriptions record a wide range of intermediate appearances during the transition between breeding and nonbreeding plumages (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pheasant-tailed Jacana is reported from freshwater wetlands.

The Comb-crested Jacana is a small, long-toed waterbird with a distinctive red fleshy crest above the forehead and a dark breast. Its greatly elongated toes allow it to stand and move across floating wetland vegetation. The crest and exceptionally long toes distinguish adults from other small wetland birds (BirdLife Australia, 2020). The Comb-crested Jacana has been documented on Mindanao, including Sultan Kudarat and Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). Comb-crested Jacanas walk across floating vegetation using elongated toes while taking insects and other small aquatic animals (Parks Australia, n.d.). The Comb-crested Jacana is reported from freshwater wetlands. AVONET lists a culmen length of 28.1 mm, wing length of 135.1 mm, tail length of 41.2 mm, and body mass of 98.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 3.4 mm, bill depth of 5.2 mm, and tarsus length of 58.9 mm for Irediparra gallinacea (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 14.6 mm, Kipp’s distance of 43.9 mm and wing length of 135.1 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 32.5 (Tobias et al., 2022).

Parks Australia. (n.d.). Comb-crested Jacana. Kakadu National Park. https://kakadu.gov.au/discover/nature/birds/comb-crested-jacana/

records.p: A nonbreeding Whiskered Tern has a grey rump, relatively sturdy bill and narrow white hindneck collar, compared with White-winged Tern (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Whiskered Tern has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur, Davao del Norte, and Davao del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Whiskered Tern is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as rivers and streams. The Whiskered Tern takes food by skimming or dipping to the water surface, only rarely plunge-diving (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Bourns and Worcester reported flocks feeding over rice paddies on Mindanao, illustrating inland foraging during Philippine occurrence (McGregor, 1909–1910).

In breeding plumage the black body contrasts sharply with white upperwings and tail. Nonbreeding birds have a broad white collar and a dark mark behind each ear (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-winged Tern is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur, South Cotabato, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-winged Tern takes food at the water surface, skimming and contact-dipping in loose flocks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-winged Tern is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

records.p: Nonbreeding adults have a white head with a dark ear spot; breeding birds have a chocolate-brown hood. A broad white flash on the outer wing is conspicuous in flight (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-headed Gull has been documented on Mindanao, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black-headed Gull has a varied diet including invertebrates, fish and plant matter; birds may gather around fishing vessels (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-headed Gull is reported from freshwater wetlands, agricultural areas, settlements and disturbed habitats, as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 42.1 mm, wing length of 308.1 mm, tail length of 123.5 mm, and body mass of 218.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 6.2 mm, bill depth of 10.8 mm, and tarsus length of 31.5 mm for Gelochelidon nilotica (Tobias et al., 2022). The Gull-billed Tern is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Gull-billed Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

Adult Black-tailed Gulls have a dark-grey back, a conspicuous black terminal band across the otherwise white tail and a yellow bill marked by a black band and red tip. First-winter birds are largely dark brown with a paler face, so the adult bill and tail pattern does not describe every age class (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The Black-tailed Gull is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Black-tailed Gull is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 58.7 mm, wing length of 364.2 mm, tail length of 135.4 mm, and body mass of 561 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 6.5 mm, bill depth of 14.5 mm, and tarsus length of 53.4 mm for Larus crassirostris (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 21.8 mm, Kipp’s distance of 217.2 mm, and wing length of 364.2 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 59.6 (Tobias et al., 2022).

The adult Slaty-backed Gull is a large, heavy-bodied gull with dark slate-grey upperparts, white head and underside in breeding plumage, and short pink legs. A broad white crescent near the folded wingtip and a string of pale markings between the grey and black outer primaries help distinguish adults; younger birds take several years to acquire this pattern (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Slaty-backed Gull is included among historical bird records from Mindanao (DENR-PAWB, 2004). The Slaty-backed Gull is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 68.1 mm, wing length of 435 mm, tail length of 171.5 mm, and body mass of 1323 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 9.2 mm, bill depth of 19.6 mm, and tarsus length of 68.2 mm for Larus schistisagus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 24.8 mm, Kipp’s distance of 231 mm, and wing length of 435 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 53.1 (Tobias et al., 2022).

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Larus pipixcan: culmen 39.8 mm, wing 279.4 mm, tarsus 39.9 mm and body mass 280 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Franklin's Gull is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Franklin's Gulls forage while walking or swimming and also capture flying insects; breeding colonies occupy marsh vegetation (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The Franklin's Gull is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Aleutian Tern in breeding plumage has dark grey upperparts, a grey wash on the underparts, a white rump and tail, and a broad white forehead framed by a dark cap and eye line. A dark trailing edge across the secondary feathers is useful in several plumages, especially in flight. Juveniles show dark brownish upperparts with crisp pale fringes (Carey and Pang, 2022). The Aleutian Tern is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Aleutian Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters. Aleutian Terns catch small fishes at or near the sea surface and commonly associate with other seabirds while foraging (Alaska Department of Fish and Game, n.d.). AVONET lists a culmen length of 37.3 mm, wing length of 262.2 mm, tail length of 152.4 mm, and body mass of 120 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 4.1 mm, bill depth of 6.5 mm, and tarsus length of 17.3 mm for Onychoprion aleuticus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 23.2 mm, Kipp’s distance of 185 mm, and wing length of 262.2 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 70.6 (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.short: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, n.d.
r.full: Alaska Department of Fish and Game. (n.d.). Aleutian Tern. Bird viewing. https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=birdviewing.birdersbirds&species=aleutiantern

records.p: A deeply forked tail, whitish forehead and collar, and dark mask mark this oceanic tern; younger birds show pale-edged upperpart feathers (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Bridled Tern has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Bridled Tern is reported from offshore waters. The Bridled Tern usually catches prey by dipping its bill at the water surface during low flight over open sea (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Bridled Terns commonly pick prey from the sea surface without immersing the body, sometimes foraging far offshore in small groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The black cap and upperparts, white forehead and underparts, and very long forked tail identify the sooty tern (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Sooty Tern is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Sooty Terns feed on fish near the sea surface and place a single egg in an exposed nesting site on breeding islands (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The Sooty Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Roseate Tern is slender, with long pointed wings and a deeply forked tail. Breeding adults have very pale grey upperparts, white underparts, a black cap and a narrow black bill, with orange-toned feet. Plumage and bill colour change outside the breeding season, so these characters apply principally to breeding adults (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2025). The Roseate Tern is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Roseate Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Roseate Terns capture small fish by dipping or plunging briefly into the sea, often feeding in association with other terns (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). AVONET lists a culmen length of 45.3 mm, wing length of 223.8 mm, tail length of 165.8 mm, and body mass of 112 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 3.6 mm, bill depth of 7 mm, and tarsus length of 19.7 mm for Sterna dougallii (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 28.9 mm, Kipp’s distance of 156 mm and wing length of 223.8 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 69.7 (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: Cornell Lab of Ornithology. (2025). Roseate Tern (Sterna dougallii). Land Trust Bird Conservation Initiative. https://www.birds.cornell.edu/landtrust/roseate-tern-rost/

records.p: The common tern combines a black breeding cap, orange-red bill with dark tip, and long pale-gray upperwings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Common Tern has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Davao del Norte, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Common Terns hover or circle over water before plunging for fish; both adults attend and feed their chicks (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The Common Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

A narrow black band links the eyes across the nape on an otherwise white head; adults have a slim black bill and pale grey upperparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-naped Tern has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black-naped Tern nests on bare rock or in shallow ground scrapes on offshore coastal sites (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-naped Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters.

A tiny tern with narrow pointed wings, a white forehead and yellow bill tipped black in breeding plumage (CIESM, n.d.). The Little Tern has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Tern searches for small fishes by hovering briefly and diving into shallow coastal water (CIESM, n.d.). Little Terns take small fish in shallow coastal water, often hovering briefly before plunging to capture prey (BirdLife International, 2018). The Little Tern is reported from rivers and streams as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

r.full: CIESM. (n.d.). Little tern (Sternula albifrons). CIESM Seabird Guide. https://ciesm.org/seabird-guide/little-tern/

records.p: A long, heavy yellow bill and ragged dark hindcrown identify nonbreeding adults; breeding birds develop a black cap and crest (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Greater Crested Tern has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Greater Crested Tern is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. The Greater Crested Tern forages at sea by plunge-diving or surface-dipping; prey may be swallowed in flight (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Exceptionally long red legs, black upperwings, and white head and body distinguish this stilt (McGregor, 1909–1910). McGregor’s historical Philippine account reported male wing length 220 mm and tarsus 126 mm, compared with female wing length 210 mm and tarsus 110 mm, with browner female scapulars (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pied Stilt has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Pied Stilt is reported from freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

The white spectacle-like face marking and long slightly downcurved bill are distinctive; females show richer chestnut head and breast than males (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Greater Painted-snipe has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Zamboanga del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Greater Painted-snipe is usually solitary and most active around dawn and dusk, probing soft mud or sweeping the bill through shallow water (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). In Greater Painted-snipes, females commonly defend territories while males take primary responsibility for incubating eggs and caring for chicks (National Parks Board, n.d.). The Greater Painted-snipe is reported from freshwater wetlands.

records.p: A dark rump, white wingbar and repeated tail-bobbing distinguish this sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Sandpiper has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Common Sandpiper forages along the edges of streams and shallow coastal pools, frequently bobbing the tail after landing (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Common Sandpipers are often solitary feeders and use a distinctive stiff-winged flight between feeding locations (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Sandpiper is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Nonbreeding birds are pale gray and white with a straight short black bill and black legs (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Sanderling has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Sanderling runs along the advancing and retreating surf, pecking at exposed sand (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Sanderling is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

Short-legged and rounded, with a long bill sharply downcurved at the tip and a visibly split pale supercilium (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Broad-billed Sandpiper has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Broad-billed Sandpiper searches soft intertidal mud for small invertebrates, walking slowly and probing with its bill tip (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.; BirdLife International, 2024). The Broad-billed Sandpiper is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

A relatively small head, long neck and upright posture, with a short bill and yellowish to orange legs, help identify nonbreeding birds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Ruff has records from Siargao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Ruff feeds chiefly by picking food from the surface, sometimes while wading through deeper shallow water (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Breeding male Ruffs gather in communal display arenas called leks; after mating, females incubate and raise the young without male care (British Trust for Ornithology, n.d.). The Ruff is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as agricultural areas.

r.full: British Trust for Ornithology. (n.d.). Ruff (Calidris pugnax). BirdFacts. https://www.bto.org/learn/about-birds/birdfacts/ruff

records.p: Adults in breeding plumage have an unstreaked rufous face, throat and breast (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-necked Stint has been documented on Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Davao del Norte and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-necked Stint feeds on mudflats in small groups, picking tiny invertebrates from the surface (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-necked Stint is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Long-toed Stint is a small, slender wader with pale legs, unusually long toes, a small head and a short, slightly downcurved bill. In breeding plumage it shows warm brown upperparts and fine streaking across the chest; juveniles have paler feather fringes and less warm colour on the head and breast (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, 2024). The Long-toed Stint is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Long-toed Stints pick small invertebrates from damp freshwater mud and wet grass (BirdLife International, 2016). The Long-toed Stint is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as coastal and intertidal habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 20.1 mm, wing length of 88.2 mm, tail length of 35.8 mm, and body mass of 30.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 2.5 mm, bill depth of 3.4 mm, and tarsus length of 21.5 mm for Calidris subminuta (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 15.3 mm, Kipp’s distance of 43.9 mm and wing length of 88.2 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 49.8 (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: This large knot has short legs, a pot-bellied shape and a heavy slightly drooping bill; breeding birds show a rufous band across the scapulars (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Great Knot has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Great Knot uses open intertidal mudflats and sandflats on migration and during the nonbreeding season (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Great Knots probe intertidal mud for shellfish and other benthic invertebrates, often feeding in dense shorebird flocks (BirdLife Australia, n.d.). The Great Knot is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Best separated from Pin-tailed Snipe by its spread tail, in which outer feathers widen gradually toward the middle rather than forming numerous needle-like pins (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Swinhoe's Snipe is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo, Zamboanga del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Swinhoe's Snipe feeds by probing soft, wet soil; flight calls alone are not a reliable separation from Pin-tailed Snipe (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Swinhoe's Snipe searches wet grass and soft mud with its long bill, feeding on invertebrates including worms and insect larvae (BirdLife International, 2016). The Swinhoe's Snipe is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as agricultural areas.

A substantial shorebird with a heavy straight bill and compact neck; nonbreeding birds are grey, while breeding birds develop orange-red head and underparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Dowitcher is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Asian Dowitcher is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as coastal and intertidal habitats. The Asian Dowitcher probes deeply and repeatedly into soft mud, often among flocks of larger shorebirds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A long, slightly upturned bicoloured bill, black legs, and finely barred rather than solid-black tail distinguish it from Black-tailed Godwit (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Bar-tailed Godwit is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Bar-tailed Godwit is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. The Bar-tailed Godwit uses its long bill to probe intertidal substrates for invertebrates, roosting in flocks at high tide (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

In flight the black-tailed godwit shows a contrasting black tail band, white tail base, and bold white wing bar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-tailed Godwit is recorded on Mindanao and Siargao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black-tailed Godwit is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Larger size and a longer decurved bill distinguish it from Whimbrel (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eurasian Curlew is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eurasian Curlew is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Longer and heavier-billed than Eurasian Curlew, with darker rump and densely barred underwings visible in flight (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Far Eastern Curlew has been documented on Mindanao, including Panabo–Carmen wetlands, Davao Gulf, and Davao del Norte (Asian Development Bank, n.d.; DENR-EMB Region XI, 2022). The Far Eastern Curlew uses intertidal flats and may associate with other curlews and whimbrels when feeding (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Far Eastern Curlew is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: The long curved bill and patterned head distinguish this coastal wader (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). A striped crown with dark central band accompanies a long downcurved bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eurasian Whimbrel has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Davao del Norte, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). Eurasian Whimbrels probe sand and mud with a curved bill, taking crabs and other intertidal invertebrates (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d.). The Eurasian Whimbrel is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

records.p: Nonbreeding birds are grey above and white below with an extremely fine black bill and dark facial patch; breeding females have red neck patches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-necked Phalarope has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Panabo–Carmen wetlands and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-necked Phalarope frequently swims while spinning to bring small aquatic invertebrates to the surface; nonbreeding birds are often pelagic (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The historical account describes patterned, down-covered chicks, with tawny upperparts and dark stripes across the rump (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Red-necked Phalarope is reported from freshwater wetlands, coastal and intertidal habitats, and offshore waters.

The Bukidnon Woodcock has a dark, finely mottled back marked by two parallel pale scapular lines and cinnamon-rufous notches in the wing feathers. Its cinnamon throat and breast bear broad dark barring, which continues onto the paler belly and undertail-coverts. Kennedy and colleagues compared these markings with other Asian woodcocks when describing the species (Kennedy et al., 2001). The Bukidnon Woodcock has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Bukidnon Woodcock occupies moist montane and mossy forest on Mindanao. Field observers also recorded birds at nearby clearings and forest edges, where they conduct display flights around dusk and dawn (Kennedy et al., 2001; BirdLife International, 2024). AVONET lists a culmen length of 85.9 mm, wing length of 161 mm, tail length of 58 mm, and body mass of 238 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 7 mm, bill depth of 11.1 mm, and tarsus length of 33.7 mm for Scolopax bukidnonensis (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 69.1 mm, Kipp’s distance of 32.2 mm and wing length of 161 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 20.0 (Tobias et al., 2022).
records.note: Montane and mossy forests and adjacent display sites from the original species description.

records.p: Breeding plumage is predominantly black, with pale upperpart spotting (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Spotted Redshank has been reported from Mindanao, where the Philippine Red List documents a rare occurrence (Philippine Red List Committee, 2020). The Spotted Redshank is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Spotted upperparts, long pale legs and a strong supercilium distinguish this sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Wood Sandpiper has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Wood Sandpiper feeds by probing small freshwater pools and muddy margins (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). McGregor described abrasion of pale feather edges during the breeding season, changing the appearance of upperpart spotting (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Wood Sandpiper is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Its long greenish legs and upturned bill distinguish it from Marsh Sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Greenshank has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Common Greenshank hunts small fish and other animals in shallow coastal water with rapid bill strikes (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Greenshank is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Compared with Common Sandpiper, it has longer legs, a more continuous dark breast band and a much clearer white rump in flight (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Green Sandpiper is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Green Sandpiper often feeds alone or in small groups at freshwater edges, sometimes alongside Wood Sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). McGregor described seasonal replacement of worn winter plumage through a molt occurring while birds remained in wintering areas (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Green Sandpiper is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams.

A fine straight bill and unusually long thin legs distinguish it from the heavier, up-billed Common Greenshank (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Marsh Sandpiper has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Marsh Sandpiper wades through shallow water and pecks prey from the surface, often alongside other shorebirds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Marsh Sandpiper is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

A markedly upturned bill and short orange legs distinguish this shorebird (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Terek Sandpiper has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Terek Sandpiper runs actively along intertidal edges, searching soft mud and shoreline debris for prey (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Terek Sandpiper is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Pomarine Jaeger is a substantial, broad-bodied jaeger with a relatively heavy bill and rounded head profile. Breeding adults can have broad, rounded projections of the central tail feathers and a dark spotted band across the breast. Young birds are more difficult to separate, often showing a strongly barred undertail and two pale zones on the underwing (Carey and Pang, 2024). The Pomarine Jaeger is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Pomarine Jaeger is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters. At sea, Pomarine Jaegers may seize food from other birds, catch small prey at the water surface or hunt birds in flight (National Audubon Society, n.d.). AVONET lists a culmen length of 45.8 mm, wing length of 350.8 mm, tail length of 175.6 mm, and body mass of 692.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 7.2 mm, bill depth of 12.5 mm, and tarsus length of 52 mm for Stercorarius pomarinus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 16.1 mm, Kipp’s distance of 196.1 mm and wing length of 350.8 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 55.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Small Buttonquail has finely mottled brown, black and grey upperparts with buff lines along the crown and sides of the back. Females are generally larger and more strongly colored, with a chestnut breast, white upper throat and pale belly. Males are duller. Plumage and measurements vary geographically, so these characters should be used together (Pappas, 2002). The Common Buttonquail has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Common Buttonquail is reported from grasslands, other open habitats, shrubland and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14 mm, wing length of 83.8 mm, tail length of 42 mm, and body mass of 52.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 2.2 mm, bill depth of 3.8 mm, and tarsus length of 21.9 mm for Turnix sylvaticus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 7.3 mm, Kipp’s distance of 23 mm and wing length of 83.8 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 27.4 (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: The Asian Woollyneck is a large, mostly glossy-black stork with an elongated, almost woolly white neck and contrasting white lower belly and tail. Adults have a sharply defined black crown, bare bluish-grey facial skin, a long dark bill with a reddish tip and orange-red legs (BirdLife International, 2020). The Asian Woolly-necked Stork is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Asian Woolly-necked Stork is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers, streams and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 149.4 mm, wing length of 456.2 mm, tail length of 169.3 mm, and body mass of 2061 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 18.1 mm, bill depth of 27.3 mm, and tarsus length of 155.3 mm for Ciconia episcopus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 123.8 mm, Kipp’s distance of 174 mm and wing length of 456.2 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 38.1 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Wild-type birds are grey with two black wing bars and iridescent green-purple neck feathers; feral plumages vary widely (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Rock Dove is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rock Dove is reported from agricultural areas as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. Feral populations occupy urban environments throughout their introduced range (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Metallic Wood Pigeon is a large, dark, glossy pigeon with a white throat. Its dark slaty nape, back and wings have metallic green reflections, while the forehead and lower body are purplish-grey with a lilac sheen. The bare skin around the eye is crimson, and the bill is yellow with a reddish base (Forest Department Sarawak, n.d.). The Metallic Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Metallic Pigeon is reported from forests and cultivated land. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 14 mm, Kipp’s distance of 70.3 mm, and wing length of 216.4 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 32.5 (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: Forest Department Sarawak. (n.d.). Metallic Wood Pigeon (Columba vitiensis). https://forestry.sarawak.gov.my/web/subpage/webpage_view/907

records.p: The pale cream-white body contrasts sharply with black flight feathers and a broad dark terminal tail band (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pied Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). Pied Imperial Pigeons feed on fruit including figs and palm fruits and may gather in flocks near fruiting trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pied Imperial Pigeon is reported from forests and agricultural land, as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Spotted Imperial Pigeon has greyish head and forebody coloration, with fine paler flecking or spotting across portions of the upperparts. The adult male is described with a pale crescent across the upper breast and a darker band below, while females are darker and show a less contrasting chest. Plumage also varies by sex and subspecies (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Spotted Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Tagubud, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Historical naturalists observed birds feeding on large seeds and nuts, sometimes congregating in fruiting trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Spotted Imperial Pigeon is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 25.1 mm, wing length of 209.2 mm, tail length of 120.2 mm, and body mass of 289 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 6 mm, bill depth of 5.6 mm, and tarsus length of 25.9 mm for Ducula carola (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 12.9 mm, Kipp’s distance of 76 mm, and wing length of 209.2 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 36.3 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).
