records.p: The Pink-bellied Imperial Pigeon has a whitish-grey forehead and purplish-grey crown, bronze to emerald-green back and wings, and a green breast contrasting with a pale pinkish-grey abdomen. The tail has a broad white transverse band, and the bare orbital skin and feet are bright red (DENR WildALERT, n.d.). The Pink-bellied Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Pink-bellied Imperial Pigeon is reported from forests. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 13.5 mm, Kipp’s distance of 63.4 mm, and wing length of 212 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 29.9 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

Fine dark barring across the neck and flanks contrasts with a pinkish breast and gray face (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Zebra Dove has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Zebra Dove is reported from grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas. The nest is a flimsy platform of twigs, generally holding two white eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A long graduated tail, rich chestnut underparts, and iridescence on the sides of the neck characterize this cuckoo-dove (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Cuckoo-Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Cuckoo-Dove is reported from forests.

Brown plumage carries an amethyst iridescence on the neck, with pale and dark facial stripes and a gray terminal tail band (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Amethyst Brown Dove has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Amethyst Brown Dove is reported from forests. The Hijo inventory describes a deep, hoop-like call and a low growling vocalization. The species was photographed during birding in 2019 but detected only by voice in the later survey (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

The dark brown crown, amethystine hindneck patch, pearly gray breast and ochraceous-brown lower body distinguish this pigeon (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Brown Dove has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). Historical Mount Kitanglad specimens came from transitional lowland-to-montane forest, including a stream valley and ridge, at about 1,100 m; other accounts describe birds feeding in fruiting trees (BirdLife International, 2001). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

r.full: BirdLife International. (2001). Mindanao Brown-dove Phapitreron brunneiceps. Threatened Birds of Asia species account.

records.note: Historical forest strata and recorded microhabitats, without interpreting the disputed coastal checklist classification as established habitat.

records.p: This small brown dove has a pale stripe below and behind the eye bordered by darker facial plumage, with bronze-green to purple iridescence across the hindneck and upper back. The tail is brown with a grey tip, and the legs are pinkish to red (WildAlert, n.d.). The White-eared Brown Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The White-eared Brown Dove is reported from forests. Nests recorded on Mindoro were made of twisted tendrils, supported on horizontal branches about 2–6 m above ground (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A crimson-to-purple hindcrown and conspicuous yellow breast patch interrupt an otherwise green body (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Yellow-breasted Fruit Dove is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Yellow-breasted Fruit Dove is reported from forests.

The spotted black-and-white neck patch contrasts with a warm pink-brown body and long white-tipped tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Spotted Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Spotted Dove is reported from forests edges, shrublands, and agricultural areas. The Spotted Dove feeds mostly on grains and seeds on the ground, commonly in pairs or small groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A slender brown-pink dove with a narrow black half-collar and pale edging at the tail corners (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Collared Dove has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Agusan del Sur, and Davao Oriental. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Collared Dove is reported from grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Males have a grey head, wine-red body, black hindneck collar and contrasting slate-coloured lower back; females are dull sandy brown (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red Collared Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Melibengoy, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Red Collared Dove is reported from grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas. The Red Collared Dove feeds mainly on seeds on the ground, generally in pairs or small groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A small kingfisher with bright turquoise upperparts, orange underparts and a white throat; females have reddish colour on the lower bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Pasonanca area. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Common Kingfisher is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines. The Common Kingfisher takes small fish by diving from a perch, then strikes prey against the perch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Southern Silvery Kingfisher has a black crown and wings, small white spots running back along the crown, and a contrasting white patch behind each ear. Its back and rump are silvery-white, the throat and upper breast are white, and the dark lower breast and flanks have a blue wash. The bill is black and the feet red (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Southern Silvery Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Southern Silvery Kingfisher is reported from forests and habitats along rivers and streams. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Compared with the southern Silvery Kingfisher, the Northern Silvery Kingfisher shows a deeper ultramarine to purplish-blue wash over the otherwise black breast and sides. Its dark bill and bright scarlet feet were recorded for both sexes; buff on the throat and abdomen of some specimens was considered possibly age-related (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Northern Silvery Kingfisher is recorded on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Mount Capotoan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Northern Silvery Kingfisher is reported from forests, rivers and streams. Small crabs were identified in one historical dietary observation; a specimen account recorded bright-red feet (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A very small kingfisher with a large red bill, blue upperparts and orange underparts, occurring in darker and paler plumage forms. The lores and moustachial area are orange rather than the blue or black shown by several similar dwarf kingfishers; a white throat grades into the orange upper breast (BirdLife International, 2016). The Dimorphic Dwarf Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan del Sur, Davao Oriental, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Dimorphic Dwarf Kingfisher is reported from forests and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 35.6 mm, wing length of 62.9 mm, tail length of 22.9 mm, and body mass of 21.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 6 mm, bill depth of 7.7 mm, and tarsus length of 13.8 mm for Ceyx margarethae (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

In the contemporary North Philippine Dwarf-kingfisher concept, this is a tiny rufous bird with a lilac wash over parts of the crown, ear-coverts and breast, a white throat and belly, and a blue-and-white patch on the side of the neck. The back carries a dark V-shaped mark; the bill and legs are bright red (BirdLife International, 2024). The Philippine Dwarf Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Dwarf Kingfisher is reported from forests and habitats along rivers and streams. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Adults are richly rufous with a bright red bill and bluish pale rump; juveniles are browner with dark bars below (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Ruddy Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Ruddy Kingfisher is reported from forests. The Ruddy Kingfisher feeds on fishes, crustaceans and larger insects, also taking amphibians (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Rufous head and breast, blue upperparts, a white throat, and a strong reddish bill characterize adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Brown-breasted Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Brown-breasted Kingfisher is reported from forests, rivers and streams, and cultivated land.

The enormous red bill, sandy-brown head, warm yellow-orange underside and blue back distinguish this large kingfisher (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Stork-billed Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Stork-billed Kingfisher is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and coastal and intertidal habitats. The Stork-billed Kingfisher usually hunts from waterside perches, diving for fish and crustaceans and also taking reptiles, amphibians and insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 43.4 mm, wing length of 91.3 mm, tail length of 60.5 mm, and body mass of 53 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 10.5 mm, bill depth of 10.1 mm, and tarsus length of 12.9 mm for Todiramphus sanctus (Tobias et al., 2022). The Sacred Kingfisher has been reported from Mindanao as an occasional visitor (Lepage, 2026). The Sacred Kingfisher is reported from forests, rivers and streams, shrubland, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

The male Rufous-lored Kingfisher has deep blue upperparts, chestnut lores and a narrow chestnut band on the hindneck. A pale blue line extends behind the eyes across the nape, while the lower back is bright silvery-blue and the underparts largely white. Females have a broader chestnut nuchal collar, darker upperparts and a variable fawn wash on the breast (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-lored Kingfisher has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Rufous-lored Kingfisher is reported from forests, coastal and intertidal habitats, and cave and karst environments. Bourns and Worcester recorded beetles, grasshoppers, spiders and grubs in the diet, with birds sometimes descending to the ground to feed (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The broad bright bill, blue-green head, and conspicuous pale blue wing panel identify the dollarbird (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Oriental Dollarbird is reported from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include the Zamboanga Peninsula and the Mount Kitanglad and Mount Hilong-Hilong areas. Historical records also document it on Samar and nearby islands (Lint & Stott, 1948; GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Dollarbird launches aerial pursuits of large insects from high, exposed branches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Oriental Dollarbird is reported from forests.

r.full: Lint, K. C., & Stott, K., Jr. (1948). Notes on birds of the Philippines. The Auk, 65(1), 41–46. https://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v065n01/p0041-p0046.pdf

records.p: Chestnut crown and mantle, an eye mask, and blue lower back contrast with the green underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-crowned Bee-eater has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Northern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Rufous-crowned Bee-eater is reported from grasslands and other open areas, agricultural areas, and forests edges. McGregor described nesting burrows excavated into level sandy ground, with a descending tunnel leading to an enlarged chamber (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 37 mm, wing length of 108.2 mm, tail length of 106.7 mm, and body mass of 29.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 5.9 mm, bill depth of 6 mm, and tarsus length of 10.7 mm for Merops ornatus (Tobias et al., 2022). The Rainbow Bee-eater has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Rainbow Bee-eater is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

An orange throat, blue tail and paired tail streamers characterize adults (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Green upperparts, rufous throat, blue rump and elongated central tail feathers are distinctive (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Blue-tailed Bee-eater has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Blue-tailed Bee-eater is reported from grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas. The Blue-tailed Bee-eater catches bees, dragonflies and other flying insects on aerial sorties, often beating captured prey against a perch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adults combine gray head and breast, rufous-buff belly, and a dark graduated tail edged in white (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Plaintive Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Plaintive Cuckoo is reported from forests. The species is a brood parasite; an account from Singapore documents an Ashy Tailorbird as a host (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adult Sunda Brush Cuckoos have a greyish head and brownish-grey upperparts contrasting with a warm rufous throat and underparts, together with a yellow eye-ring. Females can have a barred rufous form. Juveniles are more heavily barred above and below, so the yellowish eye-ring and pattern of barring are useful features (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Sunda Brush Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Sunda Brush Cuckoo is reported from forests. An account from Singapore documents brood parasitism involving Malaysian Pied Fantails (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Smaller and more lightly streaked across head and back than Greater Coucal, with a long tail and warm chestnut wings (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Lesser Coucal has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, Surigao del Sur, and Bukidnon. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Lesser Coucal is reported from forests. Often suns itself on an exposed branch with its wings partly spread (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The buff-colored head and neck contrast with a black facial mask and chestnut wings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-faced Coucal has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Black-faced Coucal is reported from forests.

Black plumage with a purple-green sheen contrasts with rich chestnut wings and a long tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). Within Greater Mindanao, the Greater Coucal is listed from Basilan. A separate mainland Mindanao report in aggregated occurrence data is not substantiated by the regional range given in the 2025 WBCP checklist (WBCP, 2025; GBIF.org, 2026). The Greater Coucal is reported from forests.

Rich chestnut wings stand out from the otherwise glossy black-green body and long tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Coucal has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). Historical observers found it in high grass and thick brush, with breeding reported during February and March (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Coucal is reported from forests.

A small bronze-green cuckoo with a pale forehead, barred whitish underside and red eye-ring in adult males; females have a yellow eye-ring (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Bronze Cuckoo has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Davao del Norte, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Bronze Cuckoo is reported from forests. The Little Bronze Cuckoo feeds on insects including caterpillars in tree crowns; the Golden-bellied Gerygone is a recorded brood host (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The crest, white nuchal collar, chestnut wings and long dark graduated tail characterize this cuckoo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Chestnut-winged Cuckoo has been documented on Mindanao, including Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chestnut-winged Cuckoo is reported from forests as well as coastal and intertidal habitats in the working regional checklist. A brood parasite, recorded using laughingthrushes as hosts; it may accompany mixed-species bird flocks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

White and buff underparts are crossed by broad dark bars, and the tail has a prominent black subterminal band (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Indian Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Indian Cuckoo is reported from forest and coastal environments in the regional working checklist. The male has a grey head and breast, brown upperparts and conspicuously barred belly and undertail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Oriental Cuckoo is a medium-sized cuckoo with grey upperparts and a pale, regularly barred underside in the common grey morph. Adults have a yellow orbital ring; some females are rufous and heavily barred. The broad, relatively widely spaced belly bars and extensive white across the underwing aid comparison with other cuckoos, but it can look essentially identical to Himalayan Cuckoo without vocal or biometric evidence (Lewthwaite, 2023). The Oriental Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Oriental Cuckoo is reported from forests.

r.full: Lewthwaite, R. W. (2023). Oriental Cuckoo (Cuculus optatus). In The Avifauna of Hong Kong. Hong Kong Bird Watching Society. https://avifauna.hkbws.org.hk/species/0040/006000

records.p: A gray upper body and strongly barred pale underparts characterize the adult cuckoo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Himalayan Cuckoo is recorded on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Matutum. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range, Mount Nacolod, and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Himalayan Cuckoo is reported from forests.

Male Asian Koels are glossy blue-black with a long tail, red irises and a pale greenish bill. Females are dark brown above and paler below, with conspicuous white or pale streaks and spots. Both sexes show the red eye, and males can be separated from similarly dark crows by the paler bill and longer-tailed shape (National Parks Board Singapore, 2023). The Asian Koel has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Asian Koel is reported from forest edge, shrubland, and cultivated land.

r.full: National Parks Board Singapore. (2023). Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus). Flora & Fauna Web. https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/fauna/6/7/6767

records.p: In Eaton’s comparison of Asian hawk-cuckoos, the adult Philippine Hawk-Cuckoo has a pale slate-grey head and upperparts, a small dark patch on the chin, and largely unmarked reddish-rufous underparts. A conspicuous pale patch on the tertials is present, whereas a white nape patch is absent in the adult. Immature birds can show dark spotting and streaking beneath, so the adult characters should not be applied to juveniles (Eaton, 2018). The Philippine Hawk-Cuckoo is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and Agusan del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Hawk-Cuckoo is reported from forests.

r.full: Eaton, J. A. (2018). Identification of Hierococcyx hawk cuckoos, and the first record of Northern Hawk Cuckoo Hierococcyx hyperythrus for continental South-East Asia. BirdingASIA, 30, 68–73. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333745229_Identification_of_Hierococcyx_hawk_cuckoos_and_the_first_record_of_Northern_Hawk_Cuckoo_Hierococcyx_hyperythrus_for_continental_South-East_Asia

records.p: An adult has a grey head, brown upperparts, rufous breast patch and barred white belly; juveniles are browner and strongly streaked (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Large Hawk-Cuckoo has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Matutum and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Large Hawk-Cuckoo uses wooded edges, secondary growth and mangroves on passage and during the nonbreeding season (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Large Hawk-Cuckoo is reported from forests as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Channel-billed Cuckoo is a very large grey cuckoo, darker on the wings and back, with a massive pale, downcurved bill and a long, visibly barred tail. The bill, body size and long barred tail together distinguish adults from other cuckoos (Australian Museum, 2022). The Channel-billed Cuckoo is recorded from Mindanao, where it is listed as a rare visitor (Lepage, 2026). The Channel-billed Cuckoo is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 82.8 mm, wing length of 339.2 mm, tail length of 270 mm, and body mass of 684 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 26.7 mm, bill depth of 31.4 mm, and tarsus length of 45.4 mm for Scythrops novaehollandiae (Tobias et al., 2022).

Adult Square-tailed Drongo-Cuckoos are glossy blue-black, with a slim, slightly decurved bill and a square to shallowly forked tail. White barring on the vent and undertail-coverts separates them from similarly dark drongos. Juveniles often show numerous pale spots on the head, body and wing-coverts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Square-tailed Drongo-Cuckoo has records from Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Mount Hilong-Hilong. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Square-tailed Drongo-Cuckoo is reported from forests, shrubland, and cultivated land.

The Spotted Kestrel has dark brown upperparts and paler brown underparts, with a narrow dark moustachial mark and yellow cere, orbital ring and legs. Males are described with a grey tail bearing a dark near-terminal band; females have more extensive barring and spotting, including multiple dark tail bands (Mallon et al., 2011). The Spotted Kestrel has been documented on Mindanao, including South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Spotted Kestrel is reported from grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 23.2 mm, wing length of 224 mm, tail length of 138.2 mm, and body mass of 162 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 9.5 mm, bill depth of 11.6 mm, and tarsus length of 41.5 mm for Falco moluccensis (Tobias et al., 2022).

Adults show dark slate-black upperparts with rich chestnut-rufous underparts and a paler throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Oriental Hobby has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Agusan del Sur, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Hobby is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats.

Adult males show a gray head, rufous upperparts spotted with black, and a distinct dark moustachial mark (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Common Kestrel has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026). Common Kestrels search open ground from hovering flight or an elevated perch and take small mammals, lizards and insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Kestrel is reported from grasslands and other open areas, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats.

The very small falcon has a dark upper body and face with sharply contrasting white underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Falconet has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Falconet is reported from forests as well as grasslands and other open areas. Early observers recorded repeated use of exposed tree perches and brief insect-hunting flights followed by returns to the same perch (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adults have an olive-brown back, bluish-gray underparts, strong digging feet, and mostly bare skin around the eye (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Megapode is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, South Cotabato, and Sarangani. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Megapode is reported from forests, coastal and intertidal habitats. Incubation takes place in mounds of organic material that warm the buried eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Male plumage includes prominent red facial comb and wattles, pointed neck hackles, and curved elongated tail feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Red Junglefowl is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Red Junglefowl is reported from forests. A nest recorded near Mariveles, Bataan, on 26 February 1904 occupied a shallow hollow sheltered by bushes and grass; it contained four cream-buff eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adult Hooded Cranes have a slate-grey body, a white head and neck, a small exposed red patch on the forehead and black flight feathers, tail and legs. Juveniles have tan heads. The contrast between the white neck and dark body makes adult birds distinctive among cranes (International Crane Foundation, n.d.). The Hooded Crane has an exceptional documented occurrence on Siargao Island, where a small group was photographed in 2020. This record does not indicate a regular local wintering population (East Asian–Australasian Flyway Partnership, 2020). The Hooded Crane uses wetlands, grassland and cultivated open landscapes in its wider range. The isolated historical Siargao record does not demonstrate regular local habitat use. AVONET lists a culmen length of 105.3 mm, wing length of 494.8 mm, tail length of 166 mm, and body mass of 3729.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 9.9 mm, bill depth of 15.8 mm, and tarsus length of 211.2 mm for Grus monacha (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: International Crane Foundation. (n.d.). Hooded Crane (Grus monacha): Identification. https://savingcranes.org/species/hooded-crane/

records.p: The olive-brown back and wings contrast with a slate-gray throat and chest and brown undertail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Plain Bush-hen has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Plain Bush-hen is reported from freshwater wetlands.

A red frontal shield and bill with yellow tip, white flank streak, and white undertail are field marks (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Common Moorhen is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Common Moorhen is reported from freshwater wetlands. The Common Moorhen swims and walks over floating leaves and other freshwater vegetation while feeding (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). A clutch of four eggs was recorded on Samar on 25 August 1896; the eggs were pale with reddish-brown spotting (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Buff-banded Rail has a grey eyebrow and cheeks, warm chestnut sides of the head and neck, a broad orange-buff band across the upper breast and conspicuous black-and-white barring on the flanks and belly. Juveniles have paler, less distinctly barred underparts and a less pronounced breast band (BirdLife Australia, n.d.). The Buff-banded Rail is recorded on Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Buff-banded Rail is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

Adults of the Barred Rail have a dark face and black throat bordered by a conspicuous white cheek stripe, a broad chestnut band across the upper breast, and densely black-and-white-barred underparts. The upperparts are olive-brown and the iris is red. Juveniles were described with a broader olive-brown breast band and less contrasting chin and throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Barred Rail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Barred Rail is reported from freshwater wetlands. Historical egg descriptions record clutches generally containing four eggs, or occasionally three, with brown and lilac spotting (McGregor, 1909–1910). AVONET lists a culmen length of 43.6 mm, wing length of 142.8 mm, tail length of 52.5 mm, and body mass of 280 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 4.4 mm, bill depth of 8.5 mm, and tarsus length of 52.2 mm for Hypotaenidia torquata (Tobias et al., 2022).

The white eyebrow and lower facial line frame a dark eye patch; a grey crown, orange bill and yellow legs complete the pattern (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-browed Crake has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Surigao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-browed Crake is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and agricultural areas. The White-browed Crake is most active at dawn and dusk, foraging along floating vegetation and muddy margins (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Blue-gray to slate-blue body plumage contrasts with the strong red frontal shield and bill (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Swamphen has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Swamphen is reported from freshwater wetlands. The Integrated Taxonomic Information System recognizes Porphyrio pulverulentus as a species, with Porphyrio porphyrio pulverulentus among its historical names (ITIS, accessed 2026).

A chestnut head, throat and breast contrast with dark barred abdomen and plain brown upperwings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Slaty-legged Crake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Slaty-legged Crake is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers, streams and agricultural landscapes. Partly nocturnal; migration records include birds encountering building windows at night (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Chestnut head and upper breast combine with bold black-and-white bars on the wings and underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Red-legged Crake has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-legged Crake walks slowly through wet leaf litter and shallow waterside vegetation to pick food from the substrate (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-legged Crake is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and agricultural areas.

A deep reddish face and breast, dark olive-brown back and red legs distinguish adults from other small crakes (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Ruddy-breasted Crake is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, Davao Oriental, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Ruddy-breasted Crake is reported from freshwater wetlands. The Ruddy-breasted Crake forages mostly at dawn and dusk, venturing a short distance from emergent vegetation (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A small grey-brown bird with bright yellow underparts and darker cheeks producing a hooded appearance (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Golden-bellied Gerygone has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Lake Lanao, Lanao del Sur, and Bukidnon. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Golden-bellied Gerygone is reported from forest edges, shrublands, agricultural landscapes. Frequently stays high among tree crowns and is often located first by voice; acts as a brood host for Little Bronze Cuckoo (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

In the museum-based account by Williamson, the upperparts are pale yellowish-olive, with fine streaking on the crown and mantle but an unstreaked rufous rump and upper tail-coverts. The tail feathers are relatively narrow and pointed. The description was based on a very small historical specimen series (Williamson, 1976). The Streaked Reed Warbler has a possible historical report from the Bislig area of southeastern Mindanao. The observation remains unconfirmed and does not establish regular regional occurrence (Greensmith, 1990, as reviewed by BirdLife International, 2001). The Speckled Reed Warbler is reported from freshwater wetlands and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.9 mm, wing length of 65.5 mm, tail length of 55.8 mm, and body mass of 8.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

r.short: Greensmith, 1990, as reviewed by BirdLife International, 2001

records.p: The Oriental Skylark is a small, streaked brown skylark with a modest crest and a relatively slim pointed bill. Compared with Eurasian Skylark it has a shorter tail and shorter primary projection, and the inner wing lacks the conspicuous white trailing edge of that species. These comparative characters can be subtle outside a clear flight view (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.). The Oriental Skylark has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Skylark is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands, other open habitats, shrubland and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.8 mm, wing length of 86.4 mm, tail length of 52.2 mm, and body mass of 26.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.short: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.

records.p: A small, short-billed bushlark with heavily dark-streaked grey-brown upperparts, a buff eyebrow, a rufous margin along the wing and a pale underside. The breast is commonly streaked and the overall colouring varies among regional forms. These are broad field marks of the species complex, not a uniquely diagnostic Philippine subspecies combination (State of Victoria, n.d.). The Singing Bush Lark has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Singing Bush Lark is reported from grasslands and other open habitats and shrubland. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.4 mm, wing length of 72.6 mm, tail length of 48 mm, and body mass of 23 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: The White-breasted Woodswallow has a dark blue-grey head, neck, upperparts and wings, contrasting with a clean white breast, belly and underwings. Its bill is blue with a black tip. Juveniles are browner and more mottled, with a thin cream eyebrow and warmer-toned underparts (Australian Museum, 2022). The White-breasted Woodswallow has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). A historical breeding colony along the Baco River, Mindoro, placed nests among the upturned roots of fallen trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-breasted Woodswallow is reported from forests.

The dark gray upperparts and barred lower body distinguish the Koch’s cuckooshrike from lighter related forms (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Cuckooshrike is reported from Mindanao and Basilan, and from Samar, Leyte and Bohol under the subspecies boholensis. These forms were formerly included within Coracina striata, and some older records remain difficult to assign under the revised species limits (Clements Checklist, 2024; Wild Bird Club of the Philippines, 2025). Early collectors reported insect and fruit material in individuals examined (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Cuckooshrike is reported from forests. The Clements 2024 revision distinguished Coracina kochii from the former Bar-bellied Cuckooshrike complex using vocal, morphological and mitochondrial characters; it tentatively included the boholensis population (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2024).

records.p: Male plumage has a glossy black face and throat, slate-gray body and paler pearl-gray rump; the female is mostly gray (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-bibbed Cicadabird occurs on Mindanao and Basilan, where the nominate form is recognized, and on Samar, Leyte, Bohol and nearby islands under the subspecies ripleyi. Some older observation datasets use Coracina mindanensis; those records need taxon-concept reconciliation before their mapped localities are transferred to the current Edolisoma combination (Avibase, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). Early examined birds contained fruit and seeds (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-bibbed Cicadabird is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

In the southern Philippine form historically called Lalage minor, males show a sharply contrasting black-and-white pattern, with a dark, glossy head and upperparts against extensive white on the lower back and underparts. Females are more grey or brownish and show barring on the flanks; McGregor noted geographically varying female throat and chest markings. These southern comparisons should not be generalized to the nominate form across the species range (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-and-white Triller has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Sur, and Sultan Kudarat. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Black-and-white Triller is reported from forests.

An almost uniform light-gray back contrasts with a black facial mask and breast, gray belly and white wing markings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The McGregor's Cuckooshrike has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, South Cotabato, and Sarangani (Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The McGregor's Cuckooshrike is reported from forests. The Mt. Melibengoy authors specifically identified this cuckooshrike among bird taxa warranting additional natural-history and taxonomic study; they did not formally diagnose a new lineage (Pitogo et al., 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Mindanao Tailor Warbler has a cinnamon-rufous crown, sides of the head and throat, olive-green upperparts, and canary-yellow breast and belly. Its dark wing feathers are edged olive-green. The original description was not assigned to a known sex, so the account does not presume that the plumage is identical in both sexes (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-headed Tailorbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rufous-headed Tailorbird is reported from forests.

Breeding males show a golden crown, dark streaked back and tawny underparts; females retain a streaked brown head (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Golden-headed Cisticola has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range, Mount Nacolod, and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Golden-headed Cisticola is reported from grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

A small warbler with dark-streaked buff upperparts, rufous rump and pale underside with buff flanks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Zitting Cisticola is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Zitting Cisticola usually keeps low in long grass; territorial males circle and hover in display flights during breeding (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Zitting Cisticola is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, as well as agricultural land.

A minute, very short-tailed bird with olive-green upperparts, a conspicuous yellow eyebrow and bright yellow underparts. Long, slender, white-shafted feathers on the lower back and flanks extend toward or beyond the tail tip. The bill is fine and slightly downcurved. The original Leyte series included a paler bird, but the author could not establish whether this reflected sex or age (Amadon, 1962). The Visayan Miniature Babbler is documented on Samar and Leyte. Older Mindanao reports under a broader Micromacronus leytensis concept are now generally treated as M. sordidus (WBCP, 2025; Avibase, 2026). The Visayan Miniature Babbler occurs in lowland old-growth forest on Samar, moving in small groups through the forest canopy. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The Grey-headed Tailorbird shows a slate-grey head and nape, a contrasting white patch around the ear, a black throat and pale grey upper breast. The back is olive-green and the belly is mostly whitish, with yellow-olive on the sides. Immatures have more extensive pale feathering around the throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-eared Tailorbird is recorded on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Lake Lanao, Lake Holon, and Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The White-eared Tailorbird is reported from forests. Bourns and Worcester recorded breeding on Basilan during August (McGregor, 1909–1910).

This tailorbird has a rufous-chestnut forehead and lores adjoining a contrasting ashy-grey crown. The remaining upperparts are olive, while the throat and central underparts are whitish and the breast sides can carry faint grey streaking. McGregor also described a Basilan form with rufous extending farther over the crown, demonstrating within-complex geographic variation (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-fronted Tailorbird has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rufous-fronted Tailorbird is reported from forest edge, shrubland, and cultivated land.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 17.4 mm, wing length of 51.8 mm, tail length of 47.5 mm, and body mass of 9.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Black-headed Tailorbird is recorded on Mindanao, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Bega Watershed, Mount Matutum, Mount Mayo, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black-headed Tailorbird is reported from forests.

McGregor described this Philippine crow as predominantly black, with greenish to purplish sheen on the wings and body, a stout bill and a rounded tail. Those features recognize a crow but do not independently establish the identity of every black corvid at a distance. Historical specimens were placed under Corone philippina before the modern Corvus combination (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Jungle Crow has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Jungle Crow is reported from grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. The Clements 2024 checklist split Philippine Jungle Crow from the wider Corvus macrorhynchos treatment, citing distinctions involving size, shape and vocalizations among forms. Historical Philippine records under C. macrorhynchos need assessment before reassignment to C. philippinus, especially when they do not preserve identifying subspecies or specimen information (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2024).

Mann’s taxonomic treatment describes the nominate Dicaeum aeruginosum aeruginosum as olive-green above, greener on the rump, and whitish below with conspicuous brown breast streaks and a stout bill. This is a subspecies-level literature diagnosis, not a measured character range for every Philippine population (Mann, 2002). The Striped Flowerpecker has historical records from Mindanao, including the Mount Matutum area. Under the current Clements treatment, the Philippine taxon is included within Pachyglossa agilis, so this entry overlaps with that species account (GBIF.org, 2026; Avibase, 2026). The Striped Flowerpecker is reported from forests.

In the species comparison published by Mann, adults of Dicaeum australe have a grey throat and upper breast, no broad black transverse breast band, and a narrow red stripe down the middle of an otherwise grey underside. The bill is broader, deeper and less strongly curved than that of D. haematostictum, which has a white throat and thick black breast band (Mann, 2002). The Red-keeled Flowerpecker is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Red-keeled Flowerpecker is reported from forests.

The male Bicolored Flowerpecker has nearly black upperparts with a faint metallic blue sheen and a sharply contrasting white underside, including the underwing coverts. Early descriptions also record a dark bill and legs and a red iris (McGregor, 1909–1910, reporting Bourns and Worcester). Females and immature birds should not be assigned the same pattern without further comparison. The Bicolored Flowerpecker has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Bicolored Flowerpecker is reported from forests.

The Buzzing Flowerpecker varies geographically. Birds assigned to the western Mindanao–Sulu hypoleucum group have strongly contrasting blackish upperparts and white underparts in males, with duller brown-backed females. The eastern Mindanao–Samar pontifex group is less contrasting, with dark olive upperparts and greyish underparts in both sexes. A genomic study identified three regional lineages and detected gene flow among them; their plumage differences aid regional comparison within the current species concept (DeRaad et al., 2025). The Buzzing Flowerpecker is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Buzzing Flowerpecker has been recorded in deep forest and occasionally in coconut groves (McGregor, 1909–1910).

records.p: In the older Philippine descriptions, male Fire-throated Flowerpeckers have shining greenish upperparts, a red throat and upper breast, paler lower underparts and yellow undertail coverts. Mindanao birds described under the historical name Dicaeum apo were compared with Luzon D. luzoniense as having greener-black sides of the head and brighter yellow undertail feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). These comparisons refer to historical taxonomic forms and should not be treated as universal differences within the present D. luzoniense concept. The Fire-throated Flowerpecker is recorded in montane Mindanao, including the Mount Apo, Kitanglad, Malindang and Hilong-Hilong areas. A historically described subspecies is also known from Samar, and some older records use the pre-split name Dicaeum ignipectus (Avibase, 2026; DENR-PAWB, 2004). AVONET lists a culmen length of 9.4 mm, wing length of 46.8 mm, tail length of 24.6 mm, and body mass of 5.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Olive-capped Flowerpecker combines a greenish-yellow crown and nape with dark lores and a slim dark line through the eye. In McGregor’s specimens the mantle was brownish, upper breast grey, lower underparts pale and the flanks and undertail region distinctly yellow. The apparent prominence of the eye-line and grey breast varies with viewing angle and age (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Olive-capped Flowerpecker has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Olive-capped Flowerpecker is reported from forests.

An olive-brown flowerpecker with pale, dark-streaked underparts, a stout dark bill and reddish-orange eyes (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Thick-billed Flowerpecker is recorded on Mindanao under the Clements treatment, which includes Philippine populations formerly separated as Dicaeum aeruginosum. Its Mindanao occurrence overlaps with the book’s historical Striped Flowerpecker account (Avibase, 2026; DENR-PAWB, 2004). The Thick-billed Flowerpecker is reported from forests. The Thick-billed Flowerpecker feeds in middle and upper vegetation on small fruits, mistletoes, flowers and insects; frequently jerks its tail sideways (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Dicaeum proprium: culmen 10.3 mm, wing 57.8 mm, tarsus 13.9 mm and body mass 10.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Whiskered Flowerpecker is recorded from southeastern Mindanao, including the Mount Mayo area of Davao Oriental (Ripley & Rabor, 1966; Avibase, 2026). The Whiskered Flowerpecker is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: This dark drongo has an unusually long, slender, gently downcurved bill. The tips of the outer tail feathers curve upward and inward, helping distinguish it from other drongos when the tail is seen clearly (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Under the current treatment of the drongo complex, Hair-crested Drongo records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Bohol in older datasets require reassignment review, particularly against the Short-tailed Drongo (D. striatus). The 2025 WBCP checklist places Philippine Hair-crested Drongo populations in the Sulu Archipelago rather than these Greater Mindanao islands (WBCP, 2025; Avibase, 2026). The Hair-crested Drongo is reported from forests.

Velvety blue-black plumage, shiny scaly crown and steel-blue throat spangles characterize the southern drongo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Short-tailed Drongo is recognized from Mindanao and Basilan as the nominate subspecies striatus, with the subspecies samarensis on Samar, Leyte and Bohol. The type locality of D. striatus is Pasonanca near Zamboanga, Mindanao. Earlier records under D. hottentottus striatus or a broader Hair-crested Drongo treatment should be assigned to the modern species only where their subspecies or geographic origin is clear (Avibase, 2026). The Short-tailed Drongo is reported from forests. A documented Basilan suspended nest of plant fibers held three pale spotted eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 12.4 mm, wing length of 68.1 mm, tail length of 54.9 mm, and body mass of 14.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Yellow Bunting has been documented on Mindanao, including Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow Bunting is reported from forests and freshwater wetlands. McGregor described seasonal wear and replacement of male plumage, including changes in the dark streaking of the mantle (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Red-eared Parrotfinch has a green body, bright blue forehead and face, a red crescent across the ear-coverts and side of the neck, and a red rump above the darker tail. The bill is dark to black in adults. Females generally show smaller blue and red areas, while juveniles are greener, have a duller reddish rump and a paler bill. These age and sex characters are summarized in BirdForum’s species account (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Red-eared Parrotfinch is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Red-eared Parrotfinch is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Black head and breast, rich chestnut body, grey-blue bill and dark centre of belly distinguish adults (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chestnut Munia has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Chestnut Munia is reported from forests. The Chestnut Munia feeds on grass seeds from stems and the ground, often in flocks with other munias (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The White-bellied Munia is a small heavy-billed finch with brown upperparts, a black face and throat merging into the brown crown and back, and a striking clean white belly. The dark throat-to-white-belly contrast helps separate adults from more extensively chestnut or patterned munias. Young birds and worn plumages may require additional comparisons (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.). The White-bellied Munia has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The White-bellied Munia is reported from forests.

records.p: White underparts bear prominent dark scale-like markings, contrasting with brown upperparts; juveniles lack clear scales (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Scaly-breasted Munia has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Busa Mountain Range, and Sarangani. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Scaly-breasted Munia is reported from forests. The Scaly-breasted Munia feeds socially by climbing seed-bearing grasses and can join mixed-species munia groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The smaller Samar broadbill has a purple-brown back, black face, chestnut tail, and white-striped wing (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Visayan Broadbill has records from Samar and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Mount Capotoan. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Visayan Broadbill is reported from forests. A genomic study found that Bohol specimens formed a genetic group distinct from those from Samar and Leyte (Campillo et al., 2020). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 11.2 mm, wing length of 67 mm, tail length of 54 mm, and body mass of 12 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Mindanao Serin occurs in the mountains of Mindanao, with records from the Mount Kitanglad and Mount Apo regions. Earlier publications treated it as a subspecies of Chrysocorythus estherae (Ripley & Rabor, 1961; Avibase, 2026). The Mindanao Serin is reported from forests, grasslands and other open habitats.

records.p: A compact, thick-billed bullfinch with a dark glossy crown, a conspicuously white cheek patch, dark flight feathers, a white rump and warm brown back and underparts. The inner secondaries may show a narrow orange-red edge in adult males, more yellow-orange in females. Historical Mindanao birds were separated as Pyrrhula steerei from northern P. leucogenys by a smaller, darker bill, browner body and a tendency toward a paler centre of the abdomen. These are population-level historic descriptions within the composite name used here, not a demonstrated diagnostic threshold for all Mindanao birds (Mearns, 1909, reproduced in McGregor, 1910). The White-cheeked Bullfinch has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, North Cotabato, and Davao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-cheeked Bullfinch is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.9 mm, wing length of 77 mm, tail length of 67 mm, and body mass of 19 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Glossy blue-black upperparts contrast with a rufous rump; pale underparts show dark streaking, and the tail is deeply forked (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eastern Red-rumped Swallow has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Holon, Misamis Oriental, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Red-rumped Swallow is reported from forests, grasslands and other open areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. The Eastern Red-rumped Swallow forages in the air with a slow, buoyant flight and often accompanies other swallows (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A deeply forked tail and complete dark breast-band separate it from Pacific Swallow (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Glossy blue-black upperparts, a chestnut forehead and throat, a dark breast band and pale underparts mark adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Barn Swallow is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and North Cotabato. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod, Lake Danao, and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Barn Swallow catches flying insects in sustained low swooping flight over open terrain (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Barn Swallow is reported from grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas.

The Philippine Fairy-bluebird has a heavy dark face, lores, throat and upper breast contrasted with glossy royal-blue crown feathers and deep indigo-blue back and underparts. Its wings combine black and blue, the eyes are reddish, and the tail is mainly blue with a dark central area. The degree of dark versus indigo upperbody plumage varies among named subspecies. These details are compiled in the species-level BirdForum account and require confirmation against a specimen-based regional treatment (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Philippine Fairy-bluebird has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat and Siargao. Mindanao reports include the Mount Apo and Mount Hilong-Hilong regions, the Busa Mountain Range and historical observations from the Zamboanga area (Lint & Stott, 1948; GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Fairy-bluebird is reported from forests.
