records.p: The brown upperparts and dark eye-mask contrast with a pale lower body (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Brown Shrike has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Brown Shrike is reported from forests. The Brown Shrike hunts from exposed perches and returns to cover after taking insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A large, long-tailed shrike with a black eye-mask, grey head, warm rufous flanks and black wings and tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Long-tailed Shrike has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Long-tailed Shrike is reported from grasslands and other open areas, shrublands, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. The Long-tailed Shrike hunts insects and small vertebrates from conspicuous lookout perches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A slate-gray crown with a black eye mask and an evenly barred chestnut mantle create the characteristic tiger pattern (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Tiger Shrike has been documented in the Bega Watershed of Agusan del Sur, northeastern Mindanao (Calimpong & Nuñeza, 2015). The Tiger Shrike takes insects, lizards, small birds and rodents in wooded edges and secondary growth (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

r.full: Calimpong, D. M. T., & Nuñeza, O. M. (2015). Avifaunal diversity of Bega Watershed, Prosperidad, Agusan del Sur, Philippines. Journal of Biodiversity and Environmental Sciences, 6(4), 385–400. https://www.innspub.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/JBES-V6-No4-p385-400.pdf

records.p: A stout hooked bill, gray upperparts, broad dark facial mask and pale underparts characterize adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mountain Shrike has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mountain Shrike is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Tawny Grassbird has a dull rufous-brown crown marked by diffuse dark shaft streaks, an off-white or grey-brown supercilium and a pale throat and belly. Adults of both sexes have similar plumage, although their measurements overlap rather than being identical. Juveniles show shorter dark crown streaks and a less defined buff supercilium (Australian Bird Study Association, n.d.). The Tawny Grassbird has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Tawny Grassbird is reported from forests habitats and caves and karst landscapes.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Locustella fasciolata: culmen 20.5 mm, wing 75.5 mm, tarsus 25.5 mm and body mass 27.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Gray’s Grasshopper Warbler has been recorded on Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). The Gray's Grasshopper Warbler is reported from shrubland and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Locustella ochotensis: culmen 16.2 mm, wing 69.5 mm, tarsus 24.4 mm and body mass 18.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Middendorff's Grasshopper Warbler has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Surigao del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Middendorff's Grasshopper Warbler is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as shrubland.

The Mindanao form, Locustella caudata unicolor, was originally described as Pseudotharrhaleus unicolor. In the historical female specimen the upperparts were deep rufous-brown, and the underside was brown tinged with olive, with a paler, buff-washed upper throat. The tail was about 75 mm, shorter than the approximately 85–88 mm tails reported for the nominate Luzon form in the same early treatment (McGregor, 1909–1910). This comparison concerns the recorded forms and does not replace vocal or modern population-level diagnosis (Avibase, 2026). The Long-tailed Bush Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, Mount Talomo, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Long-tailed Bush Warbler is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as shrubland. The Mt. Melibengoy bird inventory flags its local long-tailed grasshopper warbler population as deserving targeted comparative work, without proposing a formal taxonomic change (Pitogo et al., 2024).

A long tapered tail and large size distinguish this grassbird, with brown crown and strongly streaked dorsal plumage (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Striated Grassbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Striated Grassbird is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

The male Celestial Monarch has intense blue upperparts, throat and breast, a lighter bluish lower back and wings, a paler whitish belly tinged with blue, and a lilac-blue cheek area. A greenish-yellow bare eye ring and a long crest curving back over the crown are distinctive at close range. The female is generally less intensely blue and has a shorter crest (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Celestial Monarch has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Celestial Monarch is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.8 mm, wing length of 71 mm, tail length of 66.5 mm, and body mass of 13.6 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

The Rufous Paradise-flycatcher has predominantly warm rufous upperparts, including the flight feathers and tail, with a contrasting darker face and paler underbody in some ages and sexes. Tail length and ornamentation may differ by sex and maturity, and no single tail character should be used without comparison to the locally relevant Terpsiphone. This account is a preliminary external description from the BirdForum species synopsis (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Rufous Paradise Flycatcher has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Rufous Paradise Flycatcher is reported from forests.

Strong dark streaks cover the back, breast and flanks; breeding adults have a pink-red throat and face, usually reduced or absent in nonbreeding birds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-throated Pipit has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-throated Pipit walks over open ground, picking insects and occasionally seeds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-throated Pipit is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, as well as agricultural land.

The Pechora Pipit has bold contrasting pale and dark stripes along the sides of its back, prominent dark streaks across the breast and flanks, pale pinkish legs and a relatively large, pale-based bill. Its white-tipped wing-coverts and the projection of the primary feathers beyond the tertials are helpful distinctions from other brown pipits (Carey and Pang, 2024). The Pechora Pipit has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, North Cotabato, and South Cotabato. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Pechora Pipit is reported from grasslands and other open areas, shrublands, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. Historical accounts describe migrants skulking alone on forested ground rather than gathering in flocks (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Olive-toned upperparts, broad pale eyebrow edged dark and bold breast streaking distinguish it from the more open-country Red-throated Pipit (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Olive-backed Pipit has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Olive-backed Pipit feeds on the ground close to shrubs or trees and often flies into woody cover when disturbed (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Olive-backed Pipit is reported from forests.

A pale-bellied pipit with streaked grey-brown upperparts, slender bill and relatively long legs and tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Paddyfield Pipit is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, South Cotabato, and Davao del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Paddyfield Pipit is reported from grasslands and other open habitats, shrublands, agricultural landscapes, built-up and disturbed areas. Its flight is comparatively fluttering, and it rarely hovers before landing (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A long-tailed wagtail with grey upperparts and a yellow vent; males in breeding plumage acquire a dark throat and brighter yellow underside (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Grey Wagtail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Grey Wagtail forages along streams for aquatic invertebrates, continually pumping its exceptionally long tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Grey Wagtail is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 16.2 mm, wing length of 85.5 mm, tail length of 82.8 mm, and body mass of 19.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Citrine Wagtail has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Citrine Wagtail is reported from rivers and streams and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 15.9 mm, wing length of 78.8 mm, tail length of 66.5 mm, and body mass of 18.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Eastern Yellow Wagtail is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, and Surigao del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Yellow Wagtail is reported from freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

Philippine shortwings have compact bodies, short wings and tail, and a relatively long, slender tarsus. In McGregor’s historical treatments, males are predominantly dark slate to blackish and have a partly concealed white eyebrow patch, while females may have a rusty-brown head, face and throat contrasting with slaty body plumage. The old name B. poliogyna referred specifically to northern populations; Mindanao birds were described separately as B. mindanensis and B. malindangensis. Therefore this description indicates a complex under the modern broad Philippine Shortwing name and does not establish one uniform set of characters for all populations (McGregor, 1910). The Philippine Shortwing has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Shortwing is reported from montane habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 15.5 mm, wing length of 64.3 mm, tail length of 55.2 mm, and body mass of 17.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The male Philippine Magpie-Robin has a glossy blue-black head, upperparts, throat and breast, a sharply contrasting white lower belly, and white inner wing-coverts. The female is duller, with ash-grey across the forehead, throat and breast. Young birds are more sooty above and show pale spotting on the dark breast (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Magpie-Robin has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Lake Danao on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Magpie-Robin is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, shrubland, and cultivated land.

The Philippine Jungle Flycatcher was described under Rhinomyias ruficauda as olive-brown above, with a conspicuous ferruginous or rufous tail and relatively pale grey face. The centre of the underparts is whitish, while females were described as duller around the face. Tail colour and underpart tone provide initial recognition characters but should be compared with similar forest flycatchers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Jungle Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Jungle Flycatcher is reported from forests.

The male Mangrove Blue Flycatcher has blue upperparts and a rich orange-rufous throat and belly, grading to a whitish vent. The female is similar but shows white around the lores and below the eye, as well as on the chin. A regional comparison distinguishes the widespread taxon from the Chinese Blue Flycatcher by orange-rufous extending farther down the underparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Philippine subspecific variation requires local comparison. The Mangrove Blue Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, Agusan del Norte, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mangrove Blue Flycatcher is reported from forests.

The adult Turquoise Flycatcher has bluish-green (verditer) upperparts and upper breast, darker wings and tail with blue-edged feathers, and a contrasting paler lower belly. In the Mindanao population historically called Stoparola panayensis nigriloris (later Eumyias nigriloris), the lores were described as wholly dark to the feather tips, and the lower abdomen and undertail as creamy buff, in contrast to the paler lores and more whitish undertail of nominate Panay birds. The original distinction was based on specimens under older taxonomic limits and should not be used uncritically as a field key across the modern species range (Hartert, 1904, reproduced in McGregor, 1910). The Turquoise Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Turquoise Flycatcher is reported from forests.

The Cryptic Flycatcher is a small, subdued flycatcher. In a documented Mindanao comparison, adults had a pale olive-brown band across the breast and grey to greyish-pink legs. A recently fledged bird showed warmer orange-buff around the face, upper breast and flanks, pale flesh-coloured legs, a very short, pointed tail and a chestnut wing-bar formed by the greater coverts (Collins, 2016). These age-related characters are most useful when considered together; the juvenile plumage should not be treated as the appearance of all adults. The Cryptic Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Mount Pasian, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Cryptic Flycatcher is reported from forests.

records.p: The Mindanao Mount Apo form, Ficedula luzoniensis montigena, was described as Muscicapula montigena. Adult males have dark slaty-blue upperparts, a white eyebrow reduced to small patches above the eyes, ochraceous underparts with a pale belly, and reddish-brown tail feathers. The historical female specimens were similarly patterned but had a more olive-washed back and buff around the eye (McGregor, 1909–1910). These are characters of the recorded Mindanao form, not a blanket description of every island subspecies (Avibase, 2026). The Bundok Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Bundok Flycatcher is reported from forests and shrubland. The historical literature reports young birds collected in Benguet, Luzon, in July (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adult males have a yellow eyebrow and a dark upper body contrasting with yellow underside; females are browner and show variable dark markings on the throat (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Narcissus Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Matutum, and Lituban–Quipit Watershed. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Narcissus Flycatcher is reported from forests. Makes short flycatching flights for insects, often in the middle levels of trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The male Little Pied Flycatcher has a compact black-and-white pattern, with dark upperparts, pale underparts and a distinct white brow and wing markings. Females are principally brown above and pale below, lacking the male’s stark contrast. Identification should consider sex and age, because the dull females can resemble other Ficedula species; the regional form and vocalizations are important for confirmation (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Little Pied Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Little Pied Flycatcher is reported from forests. Breeding was reported in Benguet, northern Luzon, in an early account of this forest flycatcher (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Males have a deep blue back, black face and flanks, and white underparts; females are grey-brown with bluish wings and tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Siberian Blue Robin was historically listed from Mindanao under the former name Luscinia cyane bochaiensis. Its current regional occurrence has not been independently confirmed (DENR-PAWB, 2004; Avibase, 2026). The Siberian Blue Robin runs and hops through damp forest leaf litter, twitches its tail and sometimes bathes in streams (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Siberian Blue Robin is reported from forests as well as rivers and streams.

The original adult male was described with deep brown upperparts, a nearly black tail, slate-grey cheeks and underparts, a conspicuous white chin and throat, and tawny-olive undertail coverts. The exceptionally long tarsi and soft, elongated rump feathers were also noted. These features describe the original male specimen, not measured variation in females or a modern comparative key (Mearns, 1905, as reproduced by McGregor, 1910). The Bagobo Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Lanao, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Bagobo Babbler is reported from forests.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Cyanecula svecica: culmen 15.1 mm, wing 73.1 mm, tarsus 26.3 mm and body mass 17.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Bluethroat has been reported from Mindanao as a rare visitor (Lepage, 2026). The Bluethroat is reported from freshwater wetlands and shrubland.

Adult males of the philippensis form are blue above and on the upper breast, contrasting with chestnut lower underparts; females show scaly brown-grey plumage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Blue Rock Thrush has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, Agusan del Norte, and Agusan del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Blue Rock Thrush is reported from settlements and disturbed habitats. Scans for prey from a rock or other low vantage point, then drops to the ground to capture it (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A plain ashy-brown flycatcher with whitish underside, pale lores and a notably pale base to the lower mandible (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Brown Flycatcher is included on current Mindanao bird checklists as a migratory visitor. Its treatment has changed with the separation of related brown flycatchers, including M. williamsoni; earlier Philippine observations identified only as a broad brown-flycatcher complex should therefore be checked against the diagnostic basis and migration date before assigning them to M. dauurica sensu stricto (Avibase, 2026). The Asian Brown Flycatcher is reported from forests and coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Grey-streaked Flycatcher is grey-brown above and white below, with sharply defined dark streaks across the breast and flanks. It shows a pale narrow eye-ring, a whitish stripe below the moustachial line and a relatively long primary projection. Sexes look similar; first-winter birds may show pale tips to the greater coverts and fringed tertials (Diskin and Pang, 2023). The Grey-streaked Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Lobi Range on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Grey-streaked Flycatcher is reported from grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

Adult male Pied Bushchats are predominantly black, broken by a conspicuous white wing patch and white vent. Females are dark brown, with a warmer reddish-brown rump and lower body and no obvious pale eyebrow. Female Siberian Stonechats can resemble them, but typically show pale markings on the collar or wing absent in female Pied Bushchats. Plumage is strongly sex-dependent (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.). The Pied Bush Chat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Nacolod on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Pied Bush Chat is reported from grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

records.p: McGregor described a female of this jungle flycatcher under Rhinomyias goodfellowi as dark slate-grey to blackish on the head and back, with a narrow pale band across the forehead above the lores, white central underparts and buff-coloured flanks. This is a documented female specimen description, not a confirmed account of male or juvenile appearance (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Slaty-backed Jungle Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Davao del Sur, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Slaty-backed Jungle Flycatcher is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 18.2 mm, wing length of 85.5 mm, tail length of 68.2 mm, and body mass of 31.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The male Handsome Sunbird has an iridescent green forecrown, dark olive-green nape, yellow lower back and bright yellow breast. A narrow iridescent malar stripe and purplish ear patch contrast with a slim crimson margin beside the throat. The female has a yellow rump against a greener back. Mann separated this form from A. shelleyi, which has a crimson nape and red lower back (Mann, 2002). The Handsome Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Handsome Sunbird is reported from forests and shrubland. A nest record from near Paranas, Samar, on 19 July 1895 yielded three freshly laid, pinkish-white eggs with reddish markings (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 20.1 mm, wing length of 49.4 mm, tail length of 40.7 mm, and body mass of 7.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Apo Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Apo Sunbird is reported from high-elevation montane forests of Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The male Lina’s Sunbird has a dark greyish head and metallic blue highlights, a pale yellow throat stripe and upper breast, and a contrasting reddish-orange breast patch. The tail is elongated, with pale tips on its graduated feathers. Females are duller and lack the strong metallic markings (Philippine Red List Committee, n.d.; Philippine Eagle Foundation, 2022). The Lina's Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Tagubud, Mount Pasian, Davao del Norte, and Davao de Oro (GBIF.org, 2026). The Lina's Sunbird is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 22.5 mm, wing length of 52 mm, tail length of 40.1 mm, and body mass of 7.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The Grey-hooded Sunbird is recognizable by its grey head and neck, which contrast with the pale belly and olive-green back and wings. Males have small metallic olive-green patches on the forehead and ear region that are absent in females (Philippine Red List Committee, n.d.). The Grey-hooded Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Grey-hooded Sunbird is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: Male Metallic-winged Sunbirds show a metallic blue forehead and green or blue-glossed wing-coverts against olive upperparts, a bright yellow rump and yellow lower underparts. The chest has a conspicuous red or scarlet area; females lack the bright metallic and scarlet male pattern and are more olive-brown above and yellow below. The sexes should therefore be compared separately (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Metallic-winged Sunbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Metallic-winged Sunbird is reported from forests. Three slightly incubated eggs were collected near Paranas, Samar, on 26 July 1896; the shells had pinkish-gray mottling (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A small sunbird with a distinctly decurved bill, gray head, olive upperparts, yellow rump and yellow belly. Adult males have a narrow yellow stripe on the throat bordered by darker gray, a bluish-green tail and an orange patch near the front of the shoulder; females show a paler gray throat and faint streaking across the breast. Its yellow belly helps distinguish it from the Gray-hooded Sunbird. Sex and age should be considered when applying plumage characters, and field identification is stronger when supported by photographs or vocalizations (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird). The Tboli Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Tboli Sunbird is reported from forests. The Mount Melibengoy report recognizes the Tboli sunbird as a distinct species, while acknowledging its original description as a form of the Apo sunbird group. It associates the named form with high-elevation forest in Mt. Melibengoy, Mt. Busa and nearby Mt. Matutum (Pitogo et al., 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: Males have a notably grey throat above pale lower underparts and small light lemon-yellow tufts at the sides of the breast. McGregor contrasted this with the more yellow-bellied appearance of the similar Brown-throated Sunbird, A. chlorigaster. Females were described as duller, with greenish upperparts, so male throat colour should not be applied uncritically to all birds (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Grey-throated Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Misamis Oriental, and Surigao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Grey-throated Sunbird is reported from forests, cultivated land, and coastal and intertidal habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 18.9 mm, wing length of 61 mm, tail length of 36.2 mm, and body mass of 15 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Males show a brown face and throat, iridescent green back, purple shoulder and yellow underside; females are mostly olive-brown and yellow (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Brown-throated Sunbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Brown-throated Sunbird is reported from settlements and disturbed habitats. Visits flowers alone or in pairs, sometimes driving other birds away from a nectar source (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A long-billed spiderhunter with partly bare facial skin. Collar, Halley and Hutchinson (2026) distinguish the Samar–Leyte–Biliran population formerly called A. c. philippinensis by a bare pinkish-yellow band continuing from the lores over the forehead, paler lores, an entirely whitish line at the bill commissure, and a shorter tail. By contrast, eastern Mindanao A. c. clarae and western Mindanao/Basilan birds formerly termed A. c. malindangensis show dark lores and a sharply two-coloured commissural line; the study found no clear difference between those two Mindanao forms. The authors propose species rank for A. philippinensis. Because this edition retains the pre-revision composite account, these characters distinguish its regional forms rather than confirm a single species across all listed islands. The Naked-faced Spiderhunter has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Northern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Naked-faced Spiderhunter is reported from forests, shrubland, and cultivated land.

The Orange-tufted Spiderhunter has a long, downward-curved bill, olive-coloured upperparts, a muted greyish throat and breast and a bright yellow lower belly. McGregor described small orange-yellow tufts on the sides of the chest in males; the female did not show those tufts. A missing tuft therefore cannot by itself exclude a female of this species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Orange-tufted Spiderhunter has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Orange-tufted Spiderhunter is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 41.8 mm, wing length of 66.9 mm, tail length of 42 mm, and body mass of 11.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Garden Sunbird has olive-green upperparts and a slender, decurved bill. Adult males show a dark iridescent blue-black throat and upper breast above yellow underparts; females are yellow below, with a pale eyebrow and no dark iridescent throat patch. This description refers to the Philippine Garden Sunbird rather than the Australian sunbirds historically included under the broader name (Pranada, 2023). The Garden Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Garden Sunbird is reported from forests, shrublands, agricultural areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats. Early observers described a woven, pendant pouch nest with a side entrance, using plant fibers and spider silk (McGregor, 1909–1910).

records.p: In males of the Purple-throated Sunbird, the violet-glossed throat contrasts with a reddish chest, dark maroon mantle and metallic green highlights toward the rump. The female was described as olive above with a yellow-green underside and a subtle warm tint along the flight-feather edges. Iridescent colours may look black in poor light, and these male marks do not apply to females (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Purple-throated Sunbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Purple-throated Sunbird is reported from forests.

Bright golden-yellow plumage contrasts with a broad black band from the eyes across the nape and black flight feathers; bill is pinkish (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-naped Oriole has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Black-naped Oriole is reported from forests. Eats fruits and insects in trees and occasionally joins groups feeding at fruiting trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Philippine Oriole’s Greater Mindanao populations were treated historically under several names, including Oriolus samarensis in the east and O. basilanicus in the west. Those museum birds were mostly olive-yellow above with a grey throat and breast, pale lower belly often showing thin dark shaft streaks, yellow undertail region and a reddish bill. McGregor reported regional differences in throat tone and streaking. The historical forms are now commonly treated within O. steerii, and the described markings must be interpreted geographically rather than as fixed traits of all populations (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Oriole has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Oriole is reported from forests.

In McGregor’s historical Sulu specimen series, the upperparts were reddish brown with a darker crown, and the underparts were largely white with cinnamon markings on the throat, breast sides and flanks. These are original regional plumage descriptions, not a complete diagnosis of all populations now assigned to Pachycephala homeyeri (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-vented Whistler has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Sarangani. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). Historic notes describe insect feeding above ground level in wooded habitats of Tawi-Tawi and Sulu (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-vented Whistler is reported from forests.

The Yellow-bellied Whistler has an olive-green upperbody, greyer crown and face, pale throat and bright yellow belly. Some named forms have more grey across the head and chest, while young birds can show warmer brown or rufous feathering. Because the color balance differs among island populations, the overall yellow ventral plumage is not sufficient to identify an unphotographed or poorly observed whistler to species (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Yellow-bellied Whistler has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Yellow-bellied Whistler is reported from forests.

The Elegant Tit has yellow cheeks and underparts contrasted with a black cap, black throat bib and dark wings. Small whitish spots interrupt the wing, while white markings appear along the tips and sides of an otherwise dark tail. Females are generally less vivid. Cornell’s eBird treatment uses the genus Periparus for this species, whereas this manuscript follows Pardaliparus; the identification features refer to the same named bird (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.). The Elegant Tit is documented on Mindanao, Samar and Leyte. Reports from Bohol in aggregated occurrence data conflict with the 2025 WBCP range summary and remain unconfirmed (GBIF.org, 2026; WBCP, 2025). The Elegant Tit is reported from forests. Early observers recorded birds searching terminal foliage and sometimes hanging upside-down while feeding; breeding was noted on Cebu in June (McGregor, 1909–1910).

r.short: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.

records.p: A predominantly glossy black tit with a conspicuous white forehead and pale lores. Older Philippine treatments distinguished the Mindanao form by a broad white patch across the inner flight feathers, whereas other historical populations lacked a prominent white wing bar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao taxon is now treated as Sittiparus semilarvatus nehrkorni; the historical names and comparative characters require this geographic qualification (ITIS, 2026). The White-fronted Tit has been documented on Mindanao, including Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-fronted Tit is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 11.9 mm, wing length of 74.2 mm, tail length of 49.5 mm, and body mass of 18 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Cinnamon Ibon has vivid cinnamon-rufous upperparts and pale buff underparts, becoming greyer toward the lower belly, with a relatively stout, slightly decurved bill. McGregor emphasized the absence of a conspicuous white eye ring in this bird despite its superficial resemblance to small olive forest passerines. Both sexes in the historical treatment were generally similar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Cinnamon Ibon has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Cinnamon Ibon is reported from forests.

The brown crown, black cheek spot and black throat bib set it apart from several other small urban sparrows (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Eurasian Tree Sparrow is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Eurasian Tree Sparrow is reported from agricultural areas as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. The Eurasian Tree Sparrow usually gathers in flocks and feeds mainly on the ground, also visiting seeds on plants (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Mindanao Ground Babbler has a fulvous-brown crown and back, narrow black feather edging on the head and faint pale shaft-streaks on the back. Steere’s original comparative description separated it from the Basilan Ground Babbler by the more uniformly fulvous back and head rather than differences in overall size (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Striated Wren-Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Striated Wren-Babbler is reported from forests.

The Kamchatka Leaf Warbler belongs to the Arctic Warbler complex: olive-green above and pale below, with a pale eyebrow and wing-bars, it is extremely similar in appearance to both P. borealis and P. xanthodryas. Differences in colour and size overlap and cannot safely establish species from a normal field view. On the breeding grounds, its song is a comparatively short, rapid, regularly pulsing series, whereas calls are also distinctive from the two relatives; Philippine nonbreeding birds require suitably documented calls, or other direct diagnostic evidence, for confident assignment. Silent birds should remain unidentified within the complex (Alström et al., 2011; Perez, 2014). The Kamchatka Leaf Warbler is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Cinchona Forest Reserve, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Kamchatka Leaf Warbler is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, shrubland, and settlements and disturbed habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.5 mm, wing length of 66.2 mm, tail length of 47 mm, and body mass of 10.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

In the Mount Melibengoy population, photographed birds showed greenish-grey plumage and variable pale eye-rings, differing from descriptions of the usual olive-green upperparts, yellow underparts and less conspicuous eye-rings. The authors raised a taxonomic question rather than formally naming a new taxon (Pitogo et al., 2024). The Negros Leaf Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Occidental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Negros Leaf Warbler is reported from forests.

Du Pont’s Philippine bird monograph describes the Philippine Leaf Warbler as olive green above with a lighter rump and yellow supercilium. The chin and throat are whitish; the grey-white breast and belly show a yellow wash, and the undertail coverts are yellow. The upper bill is black and the lower mandible yellowish (du Pont, 1971). The Philippine Leaf Warbler is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Leaf Warbler is reported from forests.

r.full: du Pont, J. E. (1971). Philippine birds. Delaware Museum of Natural History Monograph Series, 2. https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.132269

records.p: The Japanese Leaf Warbler is an Arctic-type leaf warbler with a fine bill, pale eyebrow, olive-green upperparts and pale underparts. On average it is brighter green above and has more yellow on the throat and underside than Kamchatka or Arctic Warbler, but these plumage tendencies overlap. Its species status is supported by distinct songs and calls together with genetic and morphometric evidence. For Philippine field records, a suitably documented species-specific call is the strongest practical distinction; visual colour alone is insufficient, so silent or inadequately heard birds should remain unidentified within the Arctic Warbler complex (Alström et al., 2011; Perez, 2014). The Japanese Leaf Warbler is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Japanese Leaf Warbler is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.5 mm, wing length of 66.2 mm, tail length of 47 mm, and body mass of 10.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Philippine Pitta accounts of the erythrogaster complex describe a striking combination of warm reddish head or face, darker throat, green-to-blue upperparts and a strong red lower belly. A contrasting cobalt-blue breast or mantle band occurs in some forms, and juveniles can be far duller and spotted. The source includes historical Blue-breasted and Sulu forms under a broader concept, so these plumage elements cannot be assigned indiscriminately to every current species or subspecies (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Philippine Pitta is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Cinchona Forest Reserve on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Pitta is reported from forests.

The black facial band, green back, ultramarine wing coverts and ruddy belly with red vent identify the species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Blue-winged Pitta is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Blue-winged Pitta is reported from forests.

The Hooded Pitta complex has a green body contrasted with a dark or black head, a blue shoulder patch and bright red undertail region. Some forms also have conspicuous pale markings in the wings. Juveniles are less brightly colored. Taxonomic treatments differ in how the Philippine and wider Asian populations are partitioned, so head color, wing patches and the relevant subspecies must be checked against the current adopted checklist (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Western Hooded Pitta has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Siargao, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Western Hooded Pitta is reported from forests.

Adults described as olive-yellow above with dark flight and tail feathers edged olive-yellow. The yellow chin and adjacent jaw feathers have conspicuous dark, sometimes projecting shaft tips; the throat and upper breast are pale cinnamon-brown washed with yellow, becoming brighter yellow on the abdomen and undertail. Sexes were reported as similar. The old account used Iole everetti, and its character descriptions should not be transferred to Camiguin populations now treated separately (McGregor, 1910). The Yellowish Bulbul is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Yellowish Bulbul is reported from forests.

The Philippine Bulbul has a brownish-grey crown with pale feather edges, a reddish-brown throat and breast with white streaks, and a greenish-brown body. The lower belly and undertail-coverts are pale with a yellowish wash, and the bill is black (WildAlert, n.d.). The Philippine Bulbul is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Bulbul is reported from forests.

Olive-brown upperparts, white face and throat, dark lores and a vivid yellow patch beneath the tail identify adults (National Parks Board, 2019). The Yellow-vented Bulbul has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Yellow-vented Bulbul takes berries, small fruits, nectar and insects, feeding in shrubs and trees (National Parks Board, 2019). Historical field notes describe feeding around fruit trees and bushes in open and secondary-growth habitats; insects occurred in one specimen's diet (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A strong black breast band and black face contrast with the pale underside and broad fanned tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Pied Fantail has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Pied Fantail is reported from forests. A historical clutch of two eggs was collected on Marinduque on 8 May 1888 (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The white eyebrow and dark head sharply contrast with the rich cinnamon body and wings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-and-cinnamon Fantail has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Black-and-cinnamon Fantail is reported from forests.

This small blue fantail has a markedly dark, nearly blackish crown contrasting with brighter verditer-blue plumage over the remaining upperparts. In the original Samar–Leyte–Bohol comparison, both sexes were described as brighter blue above but darker crowned than Mindanao/Basilan Rhipidura superciliaris, whose upperparts were more cobalt-toned. The original comparison is useful for recognizing the regional forms, but the historical account does not establish a modern age-independent identification key (McGregor, 1910). The Visayan Blue Fantail is recorded on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Visayan Blue Fantail is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.2 mm, wing length of 76.8 mm, tail length of 78 mm, and body mass of 13.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Sulphur-billed Nuthatch was described with deep blue upperparts, a small white mark before the eye, pale violet-buff underparts and a pale bill. Females were described as lacking the dark line through the eye present in males. These are historical external characters rather than a modern subspecies key (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Sulphur-billed Nuthatch has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Sulphur-billed Nuthatch is reported from forests.

The Citrine Canary-flycatcher is a small flycatcher with a yellow face, throat and underparts contrasted against olive-brown or greenish-brown upperparts. The head and upper breast can look brighter than the back; at field range, overall yellow color alone is insufficient to distinguish it from other small insectivorous forest birds. This description follows a community-compiled species synopsis and requires an additional specimen-based differential account (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Citrine Canary-flycatcher has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Lobi Range on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Citrine Canary-flycatcher is reported from forests.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 27.1 mm, wing length of 134 mm, tail length of 81.2 mm, and body mass of 116.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Crested Myna has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Crested Myna is reported from grasslands and open country and settlements and disturbed areas.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 17.5 mm, wing length of 105.2 mm, tail length of 49 mm, and body mass of 28.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Chestnut-cheeked Starling has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chestnut-cheeked Starling is reported from forests.

The Mindanao form of the Short-tailed Starling, Aplonis minor todayensis, was described historically as Lamprocorax todayensis. Its plumage is dark and glossy, with purplish-blue reflections and a more violet-purple throat sheen than in the larger Philippine Glossy Starling. The wings and short tail are dull purplish-black, and the iris is ruby-red. McGregor reproduced measurements of the original female specimen, including a 95 mm wing and 59 mm tail, rather than a range-wide average (McGregor, 1909–1910; ITIS, n.d.). The Short-tailed Starling has records from Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Mount Tagubud, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Short-tailed Starling is reported from forests.

Adults are glossy dark green-black with red eyes; juveniles are grey-brown above with striking dark streaks on a white underside (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Glossy Starling has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Asian Glossy Starling is reported from forests. The Asian Glossy Starling feeds largely on fruits and also takes insects and nectar; communal roosts may contain very large aggregations (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 22.8 mm, wing length of 118.6 mm, tail length of 145.9 mm, and body mass of 110 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Apo Myna has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Toloma, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Apo Myna is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Stripe-sided Rhabdornis differs from some Philippine congeners in its relatively plain grey-brown or brown crown and nape rather than extensive white head streaking. Its upperparts have faint pale feather shafts, with narrow pale streaks on the wings, and the underparts are whitish with darker streaking along the sides (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Stripe-breasted Rhabdornis has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Stripe-breasted Rhabdornis is reported from forests.

The bare dark skin of the head contrasts with a pale gray body, black wings, and a white lower-breast area (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Coleto has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Coleto is reported from forests. Early collectors recorded feeding on fruits and nesting in cavities of dead trees (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The male Red-billed Starling has a pale creamy head, grey mantle and underparts, black wings and tail, a red bill and orange legs. The white bases of the primaries form a visible patch in flight. Females are duller, with browner head and underparts and less contrast between the pale body and dark wings (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, 2023). The Red-billed Starling is recorded on Dinagat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-billed Starling is reported from grasslands and open country, shrublands, cultivated areas, and settlements and disturbed areas. This broad classification does not indicate local habitat selection or breeding habitat. AVONET lists a culmen length of 26.8 mm, wing length of 120.6 mm, tail length of 71.8 mm, and body mass of 65 g (Tobias et al., 2022).
