records.p: The Mindanao Island-Thrush is variable across the island populations grouped within this species. Cornell’s 2024 Clements update describes Mindanao forms as mainly blackish with a greyer hood, except for the chestnut-bellied katanglad form. The nominate Negros population is brown. The species account therefore requires attention to the bird’s island and subspecies rather than one uniform plumage description (Clements Checklist, 2024). The Mindanao Island Thrush has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Occidental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Island Thrush is reported from forests.

Adult males have a grey head, bold white eyebrow and cheek stripe, orange flanks and upper breast, and a white belly; females are browner (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eyebrowed Thrush has records from Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). Visits fruiting trees and also searches for food on the ground (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eyebrowed Thrush is reported from forests.

The adult Sunda Thrush has very dark brown upperparts, darker toward the head, with little or no pale eye-stripe. The chin and upper throat are whitish with narrow dark transverse bars; the chest is pale slate grey and the dark flank feathers show large contrasting white diamond-shaped centres. The underside of the wing is distinctively patterned, with axillaries white at the base and black toward their ends. This is a historical specimen description, including an old Mindanao record; it is not a modern voucher-verified separation from every Philippine Zoothera (Seebohm, reproduced in McGregor, 1910). The Sunda Thrush has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Sunda Thrush is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 28.1 mm, wing length of 120.8 mm, tail length of 69.8 mm, and body mass of 90.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Mindanao Pygmy Babbler was described under Zosterornis plateni as an extremely small forest bird with olive-brown upperparts, a warmer reddish rump, a rusty face and throat, and light shaft streaks on the breast. Its dark facial and throat pattern contrasts with the pale streaks. The original generic combination is historical and modern generic assignment should be cross-checked (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Pygmy Babbler has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Mindanao Pygmy Babbler is reported from forests and shrubland. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Visayan Pygmy Babbler was treated historically as Zosterornis pygmaeus. Its upperparts were olive-brown, with narrow pale shaft streaks on the crown; the grey throat and upper breast showed fine white streaks against a paler belly. The pattern differs from the warmer and more rufous face and rump in the older description of the Mindanao pygmy babbler, but generic placement requires review (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Visayan Pygmy Babbler is documented on Samar and Leyte. Bohol appears in aggregated occurrence data but not in the 2025 WBCP island-range summary, so that record requires corroboration (GBIF.org, 2026; WBCP, 2025). The Visayan Pygmy Babbler is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 11.1 mm, wing length of 50 mm, tail length of 41.5 mm, and body mass of 8.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Mindanao Heleia shows olive upperparts, a browner forehead and dark lores, with a pale buff-white throat and a dull yellow-green wash below. The historic treatment under Zosterops goodfellowi specifically noted that the bold white eye ring familiar from many white-eyes is absent. Geographic variation in forehead and lower-face colour was described from Mindanao specimens (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Heleia has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Apo, Mount Matutum, Mount Mayo, and Misamis Occidental (Avibase, 2026, based on the Clements checklist). The Mindanao Heleia is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 15 mm, wing length of 65.9 mm, tail length of 49.5 mm, and body mass of 20 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.short: Avibase, 2026, based on the Clements checklist

records.p: The Rusty-crowned Babbler has a distinctly rufous crown and throat, brownish upperparts marked by pale shaft streaks and a light yellowish belly. McGregor noted white tips to some outer tail feathers. A combination of the rusty head, barred-looking upperparts and paler belly is a more useful starting point than any single isolated feature (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rusty-crowned Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Matutum, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Rusty-crowned Babbler is reported from forests.

Everett’s White-eye shows olive-green upperparts, a conspicuous white ring around each eye and yellow on the throat and vent, with a greyer or duller central belly. Plumage and eye-ring shape overlap with other Southeast Asian white-eyes, and some mainland populations historically included under this name have been reassigned. The Philippine account needs explicit comparison with local Zosterops and the current checklist concept (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Everett's White-eye has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Everett's White-eye is reported from forests, shrubland, and cultivated land.

A small yellow-olive white-eye with a conspicuous ring of white feathers surrounding each eye. The Cornell Lab’s Warbling White-eye account emphasizes this strongly marked eye-ring and yellow-olive plumage, characters useful for first recognition but not sufficient by themselves to separate every similar white-eye. Mindanao records are associated with the diuatae and vulcani forms in the checklist taxonomy (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.; Avibase, 2026). The Warbling White-eye has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Warbling White-eye is reported from forests.

The Lowland White-eye is a small, yellow-green passerine with a conspicuous white ring around each eye, yellow forehead and throat, greenish-yellow upperparts and paler grey-brown lower belly. Its short bill is dark, and the legs and feet are dark grey-brown (DENR WildALERT, n.d.). The Lowland White-eye has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindawag and Mount Matutum (GBIF.org, 2026). The Lowland White-eye is reported from forests and shrubland. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.1 mm, wing length of 52 mm, tail length of 40.5 mm, and body mass of 10 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The long S-shaped neck and gape extending beyond the eye are diagnostic (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Great Egret is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Zamboanga del Sur, and Surigao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Great Egret stalks shallow water slowly and strikes at fish and aquatic invertebrates using its pointed bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Great Egret is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Breeding adults develop orange-buff plumes on the head, neck and back (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Outside the breeding season, the plumage is largely white, with a relatively short yellow bill and dark legs. Breeding birds develop rufous-buff plumes (NParks Singapore, 2026). The Eastern Cattle Egret has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Tagubud, Lake Lanao, and Surigao del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Cattle Egret is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and agricultural areas. The Eastern Cattle Egret feeds in short vegetation in association with livestock and other grazing animals (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The wholly white plumage and elongated breeding back plumes accompany long dark legs (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Medium Egret has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Medium Egret is reported from freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

A chestnut neck with bold black longitudinal stripes distinguishes this heron (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Rufous neck and breast are vertically striped in dark slate, with black crown plumes and long pointed scapular feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Purple Heron has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Zamboanga del Sur, and Surigao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Purple Heron is reported from freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

In breeding plumage the head is pale yellow with white plumes, the breast cinnamon-rufous and the back dark slate; nonbreeding pond herons are extremely similar to congeners (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Javan Pond Heron has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Javan Pond Heron feeds on fish, frogs, insects and crustaceans around freshwater and wet fields (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Javan Pond Heron is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Adult males have largely cinnamon-chestnut upperparts and buff underparts with dark neck streaking (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Cinnamon Bittern has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lituban–Quipit Watershed. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Cinnamon Bittern is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and cultivated areas.

The species has warm chestnut upperparts marked by a contrasting dark cap and pale throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Von Schrenck's Bittern has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary (GBIF.org, 2026). The Von Schrenck's Bittern is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

The dark slaty upperparts and streaked pale throat contrast with a prominent yellowish stripe along the side of the neck (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black Bittern is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Samar, records include Mount Capotoan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black Bittern is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

A small bittern with a black crown and back in males, rich buff underparts and contrasting pale wing panels (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Yellow Bittern is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Zamboanga del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow Bittern is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

A compact grey heron with black crown and rear head plumes, a narrow dark bill and yellowish-orange legs; young birds have spotted wing-coverts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Heron has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Heron is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and cultivated areas. The IOC World Bird List treats Butorides atricapilla separately from B. striata following phylogenetic work. Older records published under B. striata may include more than one present-day species (IOC World Bird List, 2025–2026).

r.full: IOC World Bird List. (2025–2026). Species updates: Little Heron Butorides atricapilla. https://www.worldbirdnames.org/new/updates/species-updates/

records.p: Nonbreeding birds are white with a thick dark bill showing yellow at the base and greenish-yellow legs; breeding adults have head plumes and a mostly yellow bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chinese Egret has records from Mindanao and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chinese Egret feeds actively on intertidal mud, running, darting and making short flights as it pursues prey (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chinese Egret is reported from freshwater wetlands, agricultural areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

This reef heron has dark slate and white plumage morphs, with rather short yellowish legs (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pacific Reef Heron has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Pacific Reef Heron is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters.

The Japanese Night-Heron has a chestnut crown and short crest, a comparatively short stout bill with dark upper and yellowish lower mandibles, yellow eyes, and buff-brown neck and breast marked by darker streaking. The darker flight feathers end in conspicuous tawny rather than white tips. Compared with the Malayan Night-Heron, its chestnut crown, shorter crest and bill, and tawny primary tips are useful; younger birds are browner, more spotted and less chestnut-headed (HeronConservation, n.d.). The Japanese Night Heron has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Camera traps in Hyogo, Japan, recorded birds walking on the forest floor during daylight, apparently searching for terrestrial prey (Ornithological Society of Japan, 2023). The Japanese Night Heron is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams. AVONET lists a culmen length of 49.4 mm, wing length of 256.8 mm, tail length of 93.2 mm, and body mass of 527 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

r.full: Ornithological Society of Japan. (2023). The behaviour of Japanese Night Heron Gorsachius goisagi on Awaji Island, Japan, recorded by camera traps. Ornithological Science, 22(2), 161–168. https://doi.org/10.2326/osj.22.161

records.p: The adult Rufous Night-Heron has a short, stout bill, grey-black crown, cinnamon to rufous-brown back and wings, and pale underparts. Breeding adults may carry two or three long pale head plumes. Immatures are brown with buff and white spots and streaking, and are less readily separated from other night-herons (HeronConservation, n.d.). The Nankeen Night Heron has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Nankeen Night Heron is reported from freshwater wetlands, riverbanks and shorelines.

Adults have a black crown and back, gray wings, white underparts and long white nuchal plumes in breeding dress (McGregor, 1909–1910). Immatures differ markedly from adults in having a brown body with buff spotting and streaking (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-crowned Night Heron is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Black-crowned Night Heron is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines. The Black-crowned Night Heron frequently feeds from dusk through nighttime, unlike most day-active herons (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Australian Pelican is a very large, mostly white pelican with extensive black on the flight feathers and tail, a long pale bill and an enormous throat pouch. Adults have grey legs, while immature birds show browner areas where adults are black. Bill length and breeding-season pouch colours vary with age and sex (Australian Museum, 2024). The Australian Pelican was photographed along the Sarangani Bay coast of southern Mindanao in 2016. The observation is treated as an exceptional visiting record (Sarenas, 2016). The Australian Pelican is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and coastal and intertidal habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 414.2 mm, wing length of 601.5 mm, tail length of 151.2 mm, and body mass of 5505 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: Sarenas, I. (2016, October 1). Photo of the month: Australian Pelican. Wild Bird Club of the Philippines. https://birdwatch.ph/2016/10/01/photo-of-the-month-australian-pelican/

records.p: A long, slender, downcurved bill and dark iridescent plumage distinguish this ibis; breeding adults become rich chestnut with green iridescence (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Glossy Ibis has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Glossy Ibis wades in shallow water and probes soft mud for aquatic invertebrates (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Glossy Ibis is reported from freshwater wetlands as well as agricultural areas.

Adult White-tailed Tropicbirds are mainly white, with a bold black mask through the eye, a bright bill and two very long, slender white tail streamers. Juveniles lack the extended tail feathers and show dark bars on the upperparts. The black facial stripe and streamer colour help separate adults from Red-tailed Tropicbirds (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The White-tailed Tropicbird is listed among occasional birds recorded from Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). White-tailed Tropicbirds plunge into marine waters to take fish and squid; nesting occurs in sheltered rock cavities (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The White-tailed Tropicbird is reported from offshore waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 54.7 mm, wing length of 269.4 mm, tail length of 108.2 mm, and body mass of 328 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Adult Red-tailed Tropicbirds are nearly all white, with a strong coral-red bill, little black around the eye and two long, narrow red tail streamers. The upper wings lack the extensive black marking seen in other tropicbirds. Juveniles have a dark bill, heavy black barring above and no long tail streamers (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Red-tailed Tropicbird is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Red-tailed Tropicbirds feed at sea on small fish and squid and lay a single egg in sheltered ground or rock crevices (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Red-tailed Tropicbird is reported from offshore waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 70.8 mm, wing length of 330.5 mm, tail length of 99.8 mm, and body mass of 671.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Coppersmith Barbet is a small, green-backed barbet with a heavy bill, a red forehead and a red patch on the upper breast, separated by yellow on the face and throat. A black stripe crosses the eye and dark streaks mark the pale underparts. Young birds are duller and lack the conspicuous red patches of adults (National Parks Board Singapore, 2026). The Coppersmith Barbet has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Coppersmith Barbet is reported from forests.

A full scarlet crest, mostly black body and pale abdomen characterize adults; males also show red on the forehead and cheeks (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-bellied Woodpecker has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). Ants were recorded as food in specimen notes attributed to Bourns and Worcester (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-bellied Woodpecker is reported from forests.

A slaty-gray body, pale spots on the neck and scarlet cheek patch in males characterize this large woodpecker (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Southern Sooty Woodpecker has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Pasonanca area, Zamboanga del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Southern Sooty Woodpecker is reported from forests and settlements and disturbed habitats.

A small pied woodpecker with a broad pale stripe running from above the eye towards the nape, barred dark and pale upperparts and streaked or spotted underparts. Adult males bear a narrow red patch behind either side of the crown, lacking in females. Birds from Samar, Leyte and Bohol formerly called Yungipicus leytensis were described with a conspicuously white, faintly buff-washed rump. The Mindanao and Basilan form formerly called Y. fulvifasciatus had a pale buff back and rump and warmer yellowish underparts, often with comparatively smaller breast spots. These separate historical names are treated here only as insular forms within the checklist account; they do not define universal marks for all Y. maculatus (McGregor, 1909). The Philippine Pygmy Woodpecker is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Pygmy Woodpecker is reported from forests.

The male Tweeddale’s Frogmouth has rufous-brown plumage finely mottled and barred with dark brown, a narrow pale band across the mantle and two pale bands across the chest. White-tipped scapular and wing-covert feathers carry nearby dark spots. The female is less rufous and has a less sharply defined collar. McGregor distinguished it from the Javan Frogmouth by its greater size and comparatively shorter tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Frogmouth is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Frogmouth is reported from forests.

A small diving waterbird with a short bill and rounded body; breeding birds have chestnut face and neck and a pale patch at the bill base (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Grebe has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Ligawasan Marsh, Lake Lanao, and Lanao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Grebe dives quickly when disturbed and catches aquatic invertebrates and small fish underwater (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Grebe is reported from freshwater wetlands.
records.note: Direct waterbird behaviour description.; Streamlined checklist-derived habitat wording

records.p: The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is a long-winged shearwater with a pointed, wedge-shaped tail and an elongated dark bill. It occurs in both dark and pale morphs: dark birds are brown overall, whereas pale birds have grey-brown upperparts and a much paler underside. The wedge-shaped tail is more useful than colour alone for separating it from similarly dark shearwaters (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 40.9 mm, wing length of 296.8 mm, tail length of 130.4 mm, and body mass of 388 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Bulwer’s Petrel is a slim, uniformly dark-brown petrel with unusually long pointed wings and a tapered, graduated tail. A buff diagonal bar crosses the upper side of each wing near the carpal region. In flight it typically follows the sea surface closely, with short bursts of wingbeats alternating with low twisting glides. The combination of long tapering tail and upperwing bars is more useful than overall dark coloration alone (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Bulwer's Petrel is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Bulwer's Petrel is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 21.6 mm, wing length of 203.2 mm, tail length of 110.8 mm, and body mass of 99 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Streaked Shearwater is a large shearwater, brown above and white below, with a mottled or streaked brown-and-white head and a relatively pale, long bill. In flight its long wings are often held slightly bowed and its pale underwing contrasts with the dark outer flight-feather tips and some dusky underwing markings (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.). The Streaked Shearwater is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Streaked Shearwater is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as marine waters. The classification does not distinguish offshore foraging, coastal resting sites, or any local nesting evidence. AVONET lists a culmen length of 48.9 mm, wing length of 319.2 mm, tail length of 131.8 mm, and body mass of 580 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.short: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.

records.p: The Red-vented Cockatoo is predominantly white, approximately 30–31 cm long, with a short erectile crest and a pale grey bill. Red undertail coverts and the yellowish underside of the tail are useful field marks (Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources, n.d.). The Red-vented Cockatoo is recorded on Mindanao, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range and Lake Lanao. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Red-vented Cockatoo is reported from lowland forest, mangroves and coastal woodland. Elsewhere in the Philippines, it nests in tree cavities and forages in forest and nearby open habitats (Philippine Cockatoo Conservation Programme / Katala Foundation, 2017; Widdman, 2001; McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: A compact, mostly yellow-green parrot with a short tail and contrasting blue on the face and throat. In the Mindanao form mindanensis, males have green cheeks separating the blue around the eyes from the blue throat and show a stronger blue collar. Females have a more yellow-green head and less extensive blue facial colour (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Guaiabero is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Guaiabero is reported from forest in the regional working checklist, which also includes karst landscapes among its broad habitat categories.

The Mindanao Racket-tail has a mainly green body with brown-washed upperparts, an olive-green underside and pale blue on the forehead and around the eyes. The elongated central tail feathers terminate in black racquets. Unlike the Blue-crowned Racket-tail, the blue is concentrated around the face rather than forming an extensive deep-blue crown; juveniles lack the fully formed tail racquets (World Parrot Trust, n.d.). The Mindanao Racket-tail has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Mount Toloma, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). Historical accounts place the Mindanao Racket-tail principally in humid montane forest, especially above 1,000 m, with lower-altitude records also reported on Mindanao (CITES, 2000). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

r.full: CITES. (2000). Proposal and supporting account for the Mindanao racquet-tail, Prioniturus waterstradti; montane forest distribution and field records.

records.note: Upland forest context from a historical specialist conservation account.

records.p: Bright blue crown, green body, multicolored blue-and-gold upperwing, and red upper mandible distinguish adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Blue-naped Parrot has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Matutum, and Cotabato. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range, Mount Nacolod, and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Blue-naped Parrot is reported from forests. Nesting was reported in natural holes and abandoned woodpecker cavities in dead trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

The exceptionally deep robust red bill and green head distinguish this large parrot from smaller related species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Great-billed Parrot has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Great-billed Parrot is reported from forests and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 27.3 mm, wing length of 297.2 mm, tail length of 146.5 mm, and body mass of 322.6 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Short-eared Owl appears in historical Philippine wildlife records that include Mindanao. Regular occurrence on the island has not been established (DENR-PAWB, 2004). The Short-eared Owl is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Bubo philippensis: culmen 47.5 mm, wing 341.2 mm, tarsus 67.5 mm and body mass 532.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Philippine Eagle-Owl has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, and Busa Mountain Range. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Eagle-Owl is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

A brown owl with large yellow eyes and pale underparts marked by relatively narrow, elongated teardrop-shaped brown spots (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Northern Boobook has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Tagubud, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao de Oro. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Northern Boobook is reported from forests. The Northern Boobook hunts at night from perches, striking prey on the ground or in foliage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Compared with Northern Boobook, the dark marks on its pale underside are broader and heart-shaped; both have yellow eyes and brown plumage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Brown Boobook has a small number of reports from Mindanao and Samar in aggregated records. The 2025 WBCP range summary emphasizes Palawan, whereas the 2026 Avibase Mindanao checklist includes the species, so these records should be regarded as exceptional pending confirmation (GBIF.org, 2026; WBCP, 2025; Avibase, 2026). The Brown Boobook is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, and coastal and intertidal habitats. The Brown Boobook hunts from perches at dusk and during the night, and pairs may call in duet (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Mindanao Boobook has a spotted crown, a breast with irregular dark barring and mottling, and a paler belly marked by longitudinal dark streaks. Long, conspicuous ear-covert extensions and a low-pitched, mellow two-noted song help distinguish it from other Philippine boobooks (Rasmussen et al., 2012). The Mindanao Boobook has been documented on Mindanao, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Lake Holon, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). Historical records describe daytime concealment among dense vines and bushes; beetles and grasshoppers were recorded as prey (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Boobook is reported from forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 24.5 mm, wing length of 177.5 mm, tail length of 82.1 mm, and body mass of 137 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

An ear-tufted scops owl with dark rich-brown upperparts, a pale forehead and superciliary stripes continuing around the nape, and a dark postocular stripe extending into the ear tufts. The lower plumage is ruddier brown with irregular dark markings rather than regularly barred abdominal feathers in the historical comparison. These are Tweeddale’s specimen-based characters, not a verified modern key to every Philippine Otus (Tweeddale, 1878, reproduced in McGregor, 1909). The Everett's Scops Owl has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Everett's Scops Owl is reported from forests.

The Giant Scops Owl is a comparatively large scops owl with well-developed ear tufts, dark eyes and a rufous facial disc edged by contrasting dark and pale feathers. The underparts are warm buff to rufous, marked with strong dark longitudinal streaks. Its size and facial pattern help separate it from smaller Philippine scops owls, but an observation requires comparison with geographic congeners and variation in age and plumage (BirdLife International, 2017). The Giant Scops Owl is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Lindasan, Mount Pasian, Lake Lanao, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Giant Scops Owl is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

This small scops owl was historically distinguished from the Luzon Scops Owl under the name Otus scops mirus. The Mindanao specimens were described as having more heavily streaked upperparts, a lighter belly and a smaller size than the comparative Luzon form. These are comparative museum characters, and poorly seen owls require vocal and contextual evidence (duPont, 1971, summarizing Ripley and Rabor’s 1968 description). The Mindanao Scops Owl has been documented on Mindanao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Mindanao Scops Owl is reported from forests.

records.p: The Eastern Grass Owl has a broad facial disc, long legs and a slender, long-winged appearance. Adults have a pale buff to whitish disc and underparts, with females on average more richly buff and more strongly spotted than males. Compared with Barn Owls, Grass Owls have relatively long legs and reduced feathering over the lower tarsus and toes (Australian Bird Study Association, n.d.). The Eastern Grass Owl is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Eastern Grass Owl is reported from grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

An exceptionally long slender neck, sharply pointed bill and white streaks on the folded dark wings identify this darter (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Oriental Darter has been documented on Mindanao, including Lake Lanao and Lanao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Darter is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands. An early account recorded breeding around Lake Naujan, Mindoro, and use of freshwater streams elsewhere on that island (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Adult males are black with a white patch on each flank, while adult females show a broad white breast and collar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Lesser Frigatebird has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Lesser Frigatebird is reported from shrublands, coastal and intertidal habitats, and offshore waters. Historical observers encountered birds flying singly or in small flocks over Philippine marine waters (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Great Frigatebird is a large, long-winged seabird with sharply bent, pointed wings, a hooked bill and a deeply forked tail. Adult males are nearly black and show a red inflatable throat sac in display; adult females have a contrasting white breast. Young birds have extensive white on the head, neck and breast. The folded tail can look pointed in flight (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Great Frigatebird has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Great Frigatebird is reported from shrubland, coastal and intertidal habitats, and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 116.8 mm, wing length of 567.8 mm, tail length of 396.5 mm, and body mass of 1274.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Little Black Cormorant is a compact, all-dark cormorant, with entirely black plumage and conspicuous green eyes in adult birds. It is much smaller than a Great Cormorant and lacks the white underside of the similar-sized Little Pied Cormorant (Australian Museum, n.d.). The Little Black Cormorant is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Little Black Cormorant is reported from freshwater wetlands, rivers and other open or cultivated landscapes in the regional working checklist. AVONET lists a culmen length of 51.9 mm, wing length of 248.8 mm, tail length of 128.8 mm, and body mass of 995 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: Adults have dark chocolate-brown head, chest, upperparts and wings sharply divided from a white belly (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Brown Booby has records from Mindanao, Bohol, and Siargao (GBIF.org, 2026). Brown Boobies capture fish and squid in headfirst plunge dives into the sea (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The Brown Booby is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 79.3 mm, wing length of 366.8 mm, tail length of 193.8 mm, and body mass of 1031.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Red-footed Booby is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Red-footed Booby is reported from marine waters.

The male Philippine Trogon has a deep reddish-purple crown, black forehead and throat, bright scarlet breast and belly, orange-brown upperparts and finely barred black wings. Its outer tail feathers are extensively white with black bases. The female lacks the purple crown and scarlet underside, showing an olive-brown head and upperparts with buff underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Trogon has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Trogon is reported from forests.

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 35 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Günther's Wrinkled Tree Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). In Agusan peat-swamp forest, calling frogs perched 1–3 m above the ground, while a northeastern Leyte survey recorded calling males on ferns, small branches and other low vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2026; Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Notable identification characters include a relatively large body and broadly expanded terminal finger discs (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Rabor's Horned Tree Frog is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026; Diesmos et al., 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016; AMNH, n.d.). Rabor’s Horned Tree Frog often calls high in the forest canopy, producing slowly repeated pulsed notes; Taguibo Watershed surveys also document it on vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2016; Sanguila et al., 2021). Compiled profiles describe activity on the ground and in vegetation, with direct development rather than a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).
records.note: Combine redundant canopy statements while retaining vocal and arboreal habitat detail.

records.p: In the Asian bullfrog complex this is a robust, heavily wrinkled species with prominent dorsal ridges, dark blotches and extensively webbed hind feet; identification in Philippine invaded habitats must also consider similarly named historic H. rugulosus records and the currently accepted species concept (Frost, 2026). The East Asian Bullfrog has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The East Asian Bullfrog is reported from cultivated areas. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The revised fanged-frog complex is differentiated using comparative characters and geographic locality (Abraham et al., 2021). The Tinuy-an account describes a large frog with a conspicuous tympanum, rounded snout and fully webbed feet (Plaza et al., 2025). The Mindanao Fanged Frog has records across Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat and Siargao. Mindanao localities include the Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Balatukan, Mount Lumot, Mount Hamiguitan and Mount Malindang ranges, as well as the Pasonanca area of the Zamboanga Peninsula. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Mount Huraw; on Bohol, Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017; Nuñeza et al., 2010; Diesmos et al., 2026). A 2025 anuran survey along Miral River in Bansalan, Davao del Sur, reports the species in a six-species field assemblage (Ubat, 2025). At Tinuy-an Falls Protected Landscape, individuals were observed in small, shallow forest streams and along their banks. Other Mindanao records include ground and vegetation close to forested riparian zones (Plaza et al., 2025; Sanguila et al., 2021). The Taguibo Watershed study reported this frog from ground, arboreal and aquatic habitats, drawing on both historical and recent records (Sanguila et al., 2021). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in terrestrial and aquatic habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Stomach-content and stable-isotope analyses in a northeast Mindanao stream study supported generalist feeding on locally available invertebrate prey in the sampled Limnonectes magnus (Plaza et al., 2021). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and aquatic, with larval development. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: A comparatively large, slender stream frog with well-developed digital discs and flanks that grade from darker above to lighter below. Enlarged infracloacal tubercles occur in most examined individuals, unlike the condition reported for S. acai. Historical identification of frogs in the S. everetti complex requires attention to geographic and taxonomic revisions (Brown et al., 2017). Under the revision of Brown et al. (2017), Sanguirana everetti is associated with western and southern Mindanao. Earlier records assigned to this name from northeastern Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte require reassessment because the eastern lineage is now recognized as S. mearnsi. The unrevised GBIF records should not be interpreted as confirmed S. everetti occurrences (Brown et al., 2017). The Mindanao Torrent Frog is reported from forests and waterways. The species was described from the Zamboanga region on Mindanao, with a long taxonomic history under Rana and other combinations (AMNH, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The 2026 revision of Philippine Bronchocela diagnoses this Mindanao lineage by short, lanceolate nuchal spines, a nuchal crest of 9–12 spines separated from the dorsal crest, and narrow, strongly keeled lateral body scales. Its combination of crest and scale characters is more informative than a general green lizard appearance (Supsup et al., 2026). The Philippine Bloodsucker has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hilong-Hilong and Surigao del Norte (Tirona et al., 2026). The Philippine Bloodsucker is reported from forests and shrublands.

A photographically identified Mt. Kitanglad individual displayed vivid malachite-green coloration and ultramarine-blue ciliary scales. The lizard was not captured for detailed examination (Beukema, 2011). The Günther's Flying Lizard has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Zamboanga del Sur, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011). Fieldworkers recorded Günther's Flying Lizard in secondary-growth forest and on coconut trees beside the forest near Malagos, Mindanao (McGuire & Alcala, 2000). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A relatively large Philippine Draco with rib-supported gliding membranes. Males show a bright orange dewlap and red ventral patagia, whereas females have dark ventral patagia; body and membrane patterns distinguish it from sympatric flying lizards (Siler, n.d.). The Mindanao Flying Lizard is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Magdiwata, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Huraw, and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Mindanao Flying Lizards have been observed on tree trunks in primary and mature secondary rainforest; field accounts describe daytime activity several metres above the ground, commonly around 5–10 m (Sanguila et al., 2016). Like other Draco, it glides between trees using laterally extended, rib-supported patagial membranes (Siler, n.d.). This flying lizard lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). In Smith’s 1982 eastern Mindanao field series, a female from primary forest around 650 m elevation carried two oviductal eggs measuring 17.5 and 18.4 mm. Examined stomach contents included insects from several families (Smith, 1993). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The gliding membranes show conspicuous pattern differences between the sexes; females can be more vividly patterned than males (Uetz et al., 2026). The Ornate Flying Lizard has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). Surveys have recorded this flying lizard on trees in primary and secondary forest and in coconut plantings close to forest; northeastern Leyte records include individuals using lowland coconut-plantation vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2016; Decena et al., 2023). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Four individuals of this flying lizard were seen on a single occasion in coconut-plantation vegetation in the lowlands of the Babatngon Range, Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: This lizard has a large head, strong hindlimbs, and a neck crest generally separated from the lower dorsal crest. The base of the tail shows alternating pale and dark bands; mature males commonly have blue eyes (Sanguila et al., 2026). Lizards reported as Gonocephalus semperi have been recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Bohol. A recent taxonomic reassessment indicates that some older island records may belong to different lineages (Del Prado et al., 2026; recent Gonocephalus revision, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Anglehead Lizard is reported from forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). In the 1982 eastern Mindanao lizard collection, one female of the taxon then reported as Gonyocephalus semperi contained three developing eggs measuring 5.8, 6.6 and 7.3 mm. The same paper recorded insect and other arthropod remains in examined stomachs. This preserves the historical name and specimen scope (Smith, 1993). An archipelago-wide multilocus analysis recovered 12 putative Philippine Gonocephalus lineages, including differentiated southern island populations. The authors did not assign the available species names, including G. semperi, to individual diagnosable genetic lineages; these findings therefore cannot be converted into a verified island-by-island distribution of G. semperi (Welton et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: Taylor’s diagnosis of this slender cat snake includes an enlarged vertebral scale row and a large preocular reaching the upper head shields, in addition to the two ventral black longitudinal lines described in the baseline (Uetz et al., 2026). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The White-spotted Cat Snake has records from Mindanao (Leviton et al., 2018). The White-spotted Cat Snake is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Its midbody has thirteen dorsal scale rows, with dark longitudinal flank stripes and a pale lower-side stripe (Sanguila et al., 2026). Midbody dorsal scales number thirteen rows in examined specimens (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Bronzeback Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Agad-Agad, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). The Philippine Bronzeback Snake is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine Whip Snake is a slender, long-tailed snake that differs from the related D. rubescens in lacking the loreal scale between the nasal region and the eye. The illustrated key also reports fewer ventral scales in D. philippina, although the ranges approach one another (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Whip Snake is recorded on Leyte and Mindanao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Whip Snake is reported from forests. The original type locality of Dryophiops philippina is on northern Luzon. The Reptile Database documents its historical nomenclature and geographic records (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Ferron’s Wolf Snake has dark rings that encircle both the body and tail, unlike the incomplete dark bands of the similar L. dumerili. The illustrated key also notes approximately ten upper labial scales, of which the fourth through sixth border the eye (Weinell et al., 2019). Ferron’s Wolf Snake is documented on Samar. A separate Southern Leyte identification appears in a Mount Nacolod survey, but the specialist and national range summaries do not yet establish that island occurrence (GIZ, 2013; Uetz et al., 2026). The Ferron's Wolf Snake is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Spotted Short-headed Snake has distinct dark blotches along the back that extend down to the ventral scales. It usually has two preocular scales, a combination used to separate it from the related O. ancorus in the illustrated Philippine key (Weinell et al., 2019). The Spotted Short-headed Snake has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Norte, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; The Reptile Database, n.d.; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Spotted Short-headed Snake is reported from forests and habitats along rivers and streams. The species lays eggs (The Reptile Database, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Barred Short-headed Snake has a pale stripe along the vertebral line and conspicuous rectangular black markings on the belly, without the prominent dorsal blotches of some related kukri snakes. The illustrated key also reports fifteen dorsal scale rows at midbody (Weinell et al., 2019). The Barred Short-headed Snake was listed from Southern Leyte in a Mount Nacolod survey. That locality is absent from the 2026 Philippine reptile checklist and specialist distribution summaries, so the identification remains unconfirmed (GIZ, 2013; Uetz et al., 2026). The Barred Short-headed Snake is reported from forests. This kukri snake lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Diagnostic scalation includes absence of loreal, preocular and supraocular scales; the frontal scale reaches the margin of the eye (Uetz et al., 2026). Leviton and Brown’s published diagnosis, reproduced by the Reptile Database, records 12 maxillary teeth, an internasal contacting the upper labials, and a postocular fused to the ocular shield. These characters supplement the stated absence of several orbital shields and derive from the historical taxonomic treatment (Uetz et al., 2026). The Zamboanga Burrowing snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Burrowing snake is reported from forests. The broad classification does not establish soil, litter, or other retreat sites at named Greater Mindanao localities. Egg laying is recorded for this species (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This small Philippine snake lacks a loreal scale, and its prefrontal reaches the upper lip scales. In the illustrated Philippine key, the parietal touches both the fourth and fifth supralabials. Scales along the lowest dorsal row have dark centers and pale edges, and the brown ventral scales have paler rear margins. These characters separate it from the similar Pseudorabdion montanum in the cited key (Weinell et al., 2019). Günther’s Dwarf Reed Snake is recorded from Mindanao, alongside other Philippine islands (Uetz et al., 2026). The Visayan Light-scaled Burrowing Snake is reported from forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The historical combinations Typhlogeophis brevis and Oxycalamus oxycephalus are part of this snake’s synonymy history. A cited older name may reflect a different identification standard, so historical localities require checking against the original specimens and current diagnostic criteria (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The described head scalation includes a loreal scale but lacks a separate preocular, with seven maxillary teeth reported (Uetz et al., 2026). The historical diagnosis reported more than 30 subcaudals, anterior chin shields touching the mental, and seven maxillary teeth, based on three examined specimens. The Reptile Database lists holotype MCZ 25749 from Saub, Cotabato, Mindanao; these are type-series characters, not population-wide frequencies (Uetz et al., 2026). The Taylor's Burrowing Snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Taylor's Burrowing Snake is reported from forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine Smooth-scaled Mountain Ratsnake has smooth scales along the middle of the back and fourteen longitudinal dorsal scale rows on the front third of the body. This distinguishes it from the similar P. carinata, which has keeled middorsal scales and more scale rows there (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Smooth-scaled Mountain Ratsnake has been documented on Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Smooth-scaled Mountain Ratsnake is reported from forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The original description identifies a broad black nuchal patch, beginning several scale rows behind the parietal shields (Uetz et al., 2026). The Southern Triangle-spotted Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011; GIZ, 2013; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Southern Triangle-spotted Snake is reported from forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

records.p: This exceptionally small burrowing snake has a reported maximum total length of 172 mm and differs from related Philippine cyclocorids in body size, scalation and skeletal structure (Weinell et al., 2020). A small burrowing snake with five upper lip scales, 15 longitudinal dorsal scale rows throughout the body and single, undivided subcaudal scales (Uetz et al., 2026). The Waray Drawf Burrowing Snake has been documented on Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Weinell et al., 2020). The Waray Dwarf Burrowing Snake is a miniature, soil-dwelling snake known from Samar and Leyte. Its anatomy is adapted to burrowing, and the original species description inferred feeding on earthworms and other soft-bodied soil invertebrates (Weinell et al., 2020). The anatomical analysis suggested a fossorial lifestyle and probable earthworm feeding, but did not report direct feeding observations (Weinell et al., 2020). Levitonius was described in 2020, with L. mirus recorded from Samar and Leyte. Its diagnosis includes 15 dorsal scale rows, five supralabials and unpaired subcaudal scales (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).
records.note: Correct common-name typo and describe documented fossorial ecology.

records.p: The diagnosis notes a single scale behind the eye, incomplete snout-scale sutures and 20–23 scales around midbody; the species has the elongate, externally limbless form of a blind skink (Uetz et al., 2026). The White Blind Legless Lizard is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Lumot and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The White Blind Legless Lizard is reported from forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The type series and subsequent accounts have used several older combinations for this limb-reduced lizard, including Dibamus argenteus as a historical name associated with material from the Butuan region. These names need comparison with the original diagnoses before merging occurrence records (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Turtle-headed Seasnake has an unusual enlarged, tooth-like scale on each side of the upper lip, associated with scraping fish eggs from reef surfaces. This feature is documented in the Smithsonian’s species account and can help recognize the specialized head profile. Colour patterns and reliable separation from other marine snakes require an illustrated key and specialist examination (Smithsonian Ocean, 2015). The Turtle-headed Seasnake is recorded on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Turtle-headed Seasnake is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats as well as marine waters. This sea snake is specialized for feeding on fish eggs and is live-bearing (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The published diagnosis gives 25–30 scale rows around the neck, 39–49 at midbody, and usually a dark olive to black head and forebody with pale, oval, yellowish lateral spots; complete annuli may occur in juveniles. No single color character is sufficient for identification (Uetz et al., 2026). The Black-headed Sea Snake has historical reports from marine waters around Mindanao and Samar. Those records have not all been confirmed under modern species identifications (Leviton et al., 2018; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Black-headed Sea Snake is reported from marine waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Scale counts in the compiled diagnosis are 23–35 around the neck and 25–43 around the body. The lowermost three or four lateral scale rows are larger than adjacent rows, and dark dorsal crossbands may meet beneath the body (Uetz et al., 2026). The Short Sea Snake is recorded from coastal waters off the Zamboanga Peninsula in western Mindanao (Leviton et al., 2018). The Short Sea Snake is reported from marine waters. The species is live-bearing, rather than laying eggs on land (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The diagnostic compilation gives 27–35 neck-scale rows and 37–47 body-scale rows. The dark bluish or black bands vary in breadth and can encircle the body; band definition may fade with age, making coloration alone unreliable (Uetz et al., 2026). Live-bearing reproduction is reported for this marine sea snake (Uetz et al., 2026). The Annulated Sea Snake has records from Basilan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Annulated Sea Snake is reported from marine waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Yellow-lipped Sea Krait has a yellow upper lip, alternating dark and pale body bands, laterally placed nostrils and a laterally compressed tail. The diagnosis summarized by The Reptile Database describes 21–25 rows of body scales at midbody and broad ventral scales occupying a substantial part of the underside (The Reptile Database, 2026). The Yellow-lipped Sea Krait has been documented on Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Yellow-lipped Sea Krait is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. The category does not distinguish time spent at sea from access to coastal terrestrial resting or egg-laying sites. This amphibious sea krait returns to land to lay eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Blue-lipped sea kraits have a banded body and relatively narrow, paddle-shaped tail but must be distinguished from other Laticauda by head coloration and scale characters. In contrast to fully pelagic sea snakes, they possess enlarged ventral scales that permit crawling ashore (Uetz et al., 2026). The Blue-lipped Sea Krait is documented along the coastal reefs of Zamboanga del Norte, western Mindanao (Bucol et al., 2026). The Blue-lipped Sea Krait is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. The category does not distinguish time spent at sea from access to coastal terrestrial resting or egg-laying sites. This sea krait lays eggs on land rather than bearing its young in seawater (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Published characters include 195–205 ventral scales, 21–23 scale rows around the neck and body, and 38–43 paired subcaudals in males compared with 32–36 in females. These are comparative characters, not a complete diagnostic key (Uetz et al., 2026). The Half-banded Sea Krait has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga Peninsula (GBIF.org, 2026). The Half-banded Sea Krait is reported from coastal and intertidal habitats. Females lay eggs on land (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The body has thin lateral skin flanges and a conspicuously flattened, expanded tail. These features distinguish it from the Common House Gecko, H. frenatus, which has a rounded tail and lacks the expanded flank folds (Brown et al., 2013). The Flat-tailed House Gecko has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Agad-Agad, Misamis Occidental, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Beukema, 2011). The Flat-tailed House Gecko is reported from settlements and disturbed areas. Egg laying is recorded for the Flat-tailed House Gecko (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: In a morphological comparison that included five Philippine females, Hemidactylus stejnegeri had a strongly depressed head and body, an elongated snout and no enlarged dorsal tubercles. The paired anterior postmental scales are larger and contact one another and the adjacent lower-lip scales; the posterior pair is separated by small scales. Adhesive scansors extend along the undersides of the digits, with several subterminal scansors divided or deeply notched. The original tail has serrated lateral edges but lacks broad skin flanges. The five Philippine females measured 54.5–60.2 mm snout–vent length; this is a small sample, not a species-wide limit (Ota et al., 1993). Stejneger’s Leaf-toed Gecko has been documented from Mindanao, including museum specimens examined in a comparative study of Philippine populations (Ota et al., 1993). The Stejneger's House Gecko is reported from forests, settlements, and other disturbed areas. This gecko has documented triploid parthenogenetic populations, allowing egg production without fertilization (Uetz et al., 2026). Hemidactylus stejnegeri was described by Ota and Hikida in 1989 and had previously been treated within the H. garnotii–vietnamensis complex (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A very small slender gecko with mostly granular body scales, expanded adhesive toe pads and a conspicuous dark, approximately pentagonal marking immediately behind the hips. In the Philippine voucher series examined by Zug (2010), this postsacral marking was edged by paler areas, and living individuals had reddish dorsolateral spots. Adult males had separate series of precloacal and femoral pores, whereas adult females lacked them. Observed snout–vent lengths were 28.8–34.4 mm for 19 males and 29.6–37.3 mm for 15 females; these are sample ranges, not absolute limits. Scale and pore characters are needed to distinguish similar slender geckos (Zug, 2010). The Philippine Slender Gecko has been reported from Mindanao. Some Mindanao identifications remain subject to taxonomic reassessment. Reports from the Sulu Archipelago lie outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC (Zug, 2010; Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026). The Philippine Slender Gecko is reported from forests, rivers, streams, caves and karst areas. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Hemiphyllodactylus insularis was formerly included in the broader H. typus complex before being recognized as a separate species (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: This scaly-toed gecko has a rostral scale contacting the nostril and relatively few dorsal scales across the midbody. In the comparative series examined by Eliades et al. (2021), the two named forms, L. herrei herrei and L. herrei medianus, had 9–11 and 11–14 midbody dorsal scales, respectively. Adult males had 31–37 and 33–39 precloacofemoral pores, respectively. The recorded adult snout–vent lengths were 41.6–50.8 mm and 38.1–44.7 mm. These are measurements from the reviewed Negros and Cebu specimen series, not measurements newly verified for Mindanao records. Species-level recognition requires multiple scale characters (Eliades et al., 2021). The Negros Scaly-toed Gecko has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Agad-Agad and Lanao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; GIZ, 2013). The Negros Scaly-toed Gecko is reported from forests and freshwater wetlands. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

The comparative Philippine series of Lepidodactylus labialis examined by Eliades et al. (2021) had adult snout–vent lengths of 42.5–52.8 mm and 18–24 dorsal scales across the midbody. In the males examined, 11–13 precloacofemoral pores form a V-shaped series. Its rostral scale contacts the nostril and is cleft; cloacal spurs were absent in the comparisons, and there was no webbing between Toes II and III. The combination of rostral structure, pore arrangement and toe characters is more useful than general body colour alone (Eliades et al., 2021). The Mindanao Smooth-scaled Gecko is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hilong-Hilong and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Smooth-scaled Gecko is reported from forests, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. The species is an egg-laying gecko (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A small, smooth-scaled gecko with a greyish-tan to brown upper surface, often showing dark spots or irregular chevrons between the forelimbs and hindlimbs. A dark stripe may extend from the snout through the eye toward the shoulder. The toes have moderately expanded pads with divided terminal scansors, and the markings vary among parthenogenetic lineages (Siler, n.d., citing Brown and Alcala, 1978). The Mangrove Smooth-scaled Gecko has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mangrove Smooth-scaled Gecko is reported from forest, cultivated land and settlements and includes parthenogenetic lineages (Uetz et al., 2026). The Mourning Gecko reproduces mainly through parthenogenesis. Both diploid and triploid lineages have been described (Uetz et al., 2026). Published reproductive studies describe females producing offspring without fertilization, the parthenogenetic breeding mode characteristic of this gecko (Uetz et al., 2026). Published reproductive accounts distinguish all-female parthenogenetic lineages from rarer sexual or mixed populations of the mourning gecko. Therefore, the occurrence of eggs or several females in one shelter does not by itself establish a species-wide reproductive mode or a local breeding population (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.short: Siler, n.d., citing Brown and Alcala, 1978

records.p: An exceptionally small forest gecko in the comparative Philippine Luperosaurus material, with a robust body, conspicuous conical or spine-like dorsal and dorsolateral tubercles, lateral tail tubercles, a narrow ear opening and substantial webbing between the fingers and toes. Brown, Diesmos and Duya (2007) report 27.5–32.4 mm snout–vent length from only two examined specimens, including a possibly immature paratype, and describe roughly one-half to two-thirds webbing between the middle digits. The combination of very small size, extensive webbing, enlarged tubercles and a narrow ear opening distinguishes the reviewed specimens from many congeners. Exact pore counts are excluded here because the paper’s prose and comparative table disagree slightly on their allocation to joloensis and palawanensis. The scant material limits confident extrapolation across age classes or unexamined populations. The Jolo Wolf Gecko has records from southwestern Mindanao and from Jolo in the Sulu Archipelago, outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC. Its generic classification has also varied among taxonomic treatments (Meneses & Brown, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Jolo Wolf Gecko is reported from forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The original holotype from Jolo Island is reported as lost during World War II. This limits direct comparison with the historic type and increases the importance of examining original descriptive characters when evaluating new specimens (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A small Philippine false gecko with conspicuous pale spots along the back and sides and a contrasting band between the eyes. In the examined series, the limbs lack prominent spots and the tail lacks distinct bands. Separation from similar false geckos also depends on head and scale characters (Davis et al., 2015). The Short-footed False Gecko is recorded on Bohol and Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Brown et al., 2020). The Short-footed False Gecko is reported from forests, rivers, streams, caves and karst areas. Egg-laying reproduction is recorded (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This slender worm snake has a rounded snout, no subocular scales, nasal shields meeting behind the rostral (Uetz et al., 2026). A useful comparison with similar Philippine worm snakes is the approximately 18 longitudinal scale rows around midbody described in G. hedraeus, versus 20 reported for Ramphotyphlops olivaceus and 22 for R. suluensis in original comparative treatments. These are literature-reported differences that require correct species concept and intact specimens (Uetz et al., 2026). The Negros Island Worm Snake has been documented on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). The Negros Island Worm Snake is reported from forests. This blind snake lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The reported snout–vent length spans 58.6–83.4 mm, with five digits on the limbs (Uetz et al., 2026). The species diagnosis gives 24–27 scales around midbody and a relatively long tail (Uetz et al., 2026). The Graceful Slender Skink is documented from Mindanao. Older occurrences attributed to this name elsewhere in Greater Mindanao need reassessment following revisions of the Brachymeles gracilis complex (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026). The Graceful Slender Skink is reported from forest, although earlier island reports may refer to other members of the species complex following taxonomic revision. Ovoviviparous reproduction is documented (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The originally described female measured 71.9 mm in snout–vent length and had five digits on each limb, 24 midbody scale rows, eight lamellae beneath the fourth toe, 31 presacral vertebrae and three pairs of enlarged chin shields (Siler et al., 2012; Uetz et al., 2026). The Graceful Short-legged Skink is documented on Basilan within the Greater Mindanao PAIC. It has additional historical records from the Sulu Archipelago, outside this volume’s geographic scope (Siler et al., 2012; Uetz et al., 2026). The Sulu Slender Skink is reported from forest habitats. Its reported range includes Basilan within Greater Mindanao and other Sulu islands outside the PAIC. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A published skink comparison reports 59–63 middorsal scales and 17–22 lamellae below the fourth toe in Dasia semicincta, with the prefrontal scales usually separated. These specimen characters distinguish it from the Dasia grisea specimen compared in that study, but do not form a complete regional identification key (Geissler & Kupfer, 2019). The Half-banded Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Sinaka (GBIF.org, 2026). The Half-banded Tree Skink is reported from forests. Dasia semicincta was originally described as Euprepes (Tiliqua) semicinctus and later appeared as Dasia olivaceum semicincta. The surviving syntype identifiers include ZMB 5689 and NMW 9818; because the historical names mix species and subspecies concepts, older records require explicit name-concept matching (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A University of Guam herpetofaunal guide describes juveniles and females with three pale longitudinal dorsal stripes and a blue tail, whereas adult males may become largely brown with only faint anterior stripes. This is an external-range comparative diagnosis and has not been validated for a sampled Mindanao series (Kerr, 2013). This skink lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The Pacific Blue-tailed Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga Peninsula (Smithsonian Institution, n.d.; GBIF.org, 2026). The Pacific Blue-tailed Skink is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).
