records.p: A golden stripe runs along the dark back but does not continue onto the conspicuously reddish-orange tail (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Red-tailed Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Agusan del Sur, and Sarangani (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-tailed Skink is reported from forests and waterways. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The identity of this skink is based on type material from the Agusan region and its original description of body pattern and head scalation (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Caraga Sun Skink is a medium-sized, bronze-to-olive skink with dark sides, a long interparietal scale separating the parietals, and five to ten moderately developed keels on each dorsal body scale. It closely resembles E. multicarinata; a greater total number of toe lamellae is helpful in comparisons, but some counts overlap (Barley et al., 2020). The Caraga Sun Skink has been reported from Mindanao, Samar and Bohol, with Mindanao localities in the northeastern mountains and Agusan del Sur. Recent specimen-based records include Agusan Marsh, while older identifications in the Eutropis complex remain less certain (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Sanguila et al., 2026). The Caraga Sun Skink is reported from forests and freshwater wetlands in the working regional checklist. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Lapulapu’s Sun Skink is a relatively small, slender skink with a broad dark band along each side and five to nine keels on its dorsal body scales. Adult males may show orange coloration around the head or front of the body. Its small size and generally lower toe-lamella counts help separate it from the similar, often co-occurring E. caraga (Barley et al., 2020). Lapulapu’s Sun Skink has records from Mindanao and Samar, including Agusan del Sur and Eastern Samar. Recent specimen-based records place it in the Agusan Marsh area (Barley et al., 2020; Sanguila et al., 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Lapulapu's Sun Skink is reported from forests and freshwater wetlands. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The herrei form shows paired, unfused frontoparietal scales (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Taylor's Lipinia is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Taylor's Lipinia is reported from forests. The Reptile Database recognizes auriculata, herrei and kempi within Lipinia auriculata. Mindanao records described by Sanguila and colleagues (2016) use the herrei name (Sanguila et al., 2016; Uetz et al., 2026).

A published comparative review describes this striped skink as having longitudinal dorsal stripes that extend forward to the forelimb region, 22 scale rows around midbody, and a reported snout–vent length of 47–56 mm. The combination is useful for comparing preserved specimens with other Lipinia species (Poyarkov et al., 2019). The Striped Slender Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Striped Slender Tree Skink is reported from forests. The Striped Lipinia was originally described as Cophoscincus subvittatus and later transferred to Lipinia. Its type material came from Sulawesi, and the species is also listed from Mindanao (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

In a comparative taxonomic account, Lipinia vulcania has a brownish dorsum scattered with darker spots and a dark lateral stripe interrupted by whitish or yellowish spots. It is also described as having 17 lamellae beneath the fourth toe, with the forelimbs and hindlimbs failing to meet when pressed against the body (Poyarkov et al., 2019). The Girard's Slender Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga Peninsula (Brown et al., 2013; Uetz et al., 2026). The Girard's Slender Tree Skink is reported from forests. Historical museum literature discusses an early USNM specimen proposed as a possible type of Lipinia vulcania, following an earlier identification under another Girard name (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.full: Brown et al. (2013), ZooKeys 266:1–120 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3591760/

records.p: A small, smooth-scaled skink recorded in a comparative species synopsis at up to 44.5 mm snout–vent length, with a distinct external ear opening, 24 scale rows around midbody, 54 longitudinal scales from the parietals to the tail base and 20 lamellae beneath the fourth toe. The dorsal surface was characterized as greenish with a brown iridescent sheen. These are the reported morphological characters for Lipinia zamboangensis in Das and Austin (2007), which cites earlier Philippine treatments. Other Lipinia share parts of this combination, so a firm identification should compare multiple scalation characters; the original 1963 description was not independently reexamined here. The Zamboanga Slender Tree Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Malindang Range, Zamboanga Peninsula, and Misamis Occidental (Uetz et al., 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Slender Tree Skink is reported from forests. The Reptile Database lists the holotype as CAS-SUR 22425, from Dapitan Peak on the Zamboanga Peninsula, and records the original combination Lygosoma (Leiolopisma) zamboangensis Brown & Alcala, 1963. The type locality establishes specimen provenance, not a present-day abundance or a range-wide elevation interval (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Tinuy-an account describes large, robust adults with distinctive head scalation (Plaza et al., 2025). A large-bodied skink distinguished by its robust, elongated build (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Cuming's Eared Skink is recorded on Leyte and Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013; GBIF.org, 2026). The Cuming's Eared Skink is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A high number of paravertebral scales helps distinguish this montane skink (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Fairy Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A slender, relatively long-bodied skink with short limbs and smooth, glossy brownish dorsal scales; lateral surfaces may be finely speckled. A regional identification guide describes a transparent lower-eyelid disc, midbody scale rows numbering 24–28 and 13–14 lamellae below the fourth toe, with measured adult snout–vent lengths around 50–57 mm in its Myanmar specimen series. The coloration and dimensions reported from mainland Southeast Asia should not be assumed to diagnose every Philippine animal: the published guide itself warns of evidence for a wider bowringii species complex. Where inherited Greater Mindanao records are concerned, locality, introduction history and voucher confirmation remain separate unresolved questions (Tanintharyi field guide; Ecology Asia). Bowring’s Supple Skink has a historical report from Zamboanga, western Mindanao, interpreted as a probable introduction. Reports from the Sulu Archipelago belong to a different faunal region (Ross, 1989; Uetz et al., 2026). The Bowring's Agile Skink is reported from forests. Older literature placed this skink in Lygosoma and Riopa before its assignment to Subdoluseps (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.full: Ross, C. A. (1989). Probable introduction of Lygosoma bowringi in Zamboanga City, Philippines. Herpetological Review, 20(1), 6.

records.p: The head has four large supraocular shields, separate frontoparietal scales, and no supranasal shields; the fourth toe is only slightly longer than the third (Uetz et al., 2026). The Zamboanga Forest Skink has been documented on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area and Zamboanga del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Forest Skink is reported from forests. This skink was originally named Sphenomorphus atrigularis in 1908 and subsequently assigned to Tytthoscincus. The original holotype was collected at the base of the Malindang Mountains in 1906, providing an anchored historic Mindanao record rather than recent survey evidence (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Tytthoscincus biparietalis is assigned to a group of very small skinks, usually below 45 mm snout–vent length, with small temporal scales that blend with the surrounding body scales and a fourth toe only about as long as, or slightly longer than, the third. This species shares divided parietal head scales with T. hallieri, a feature cited in transferring it from Sphenomorphus to Tytthoscincus. The cited genus revision did not include molecular data for T. biparietalis; these characters support its generic placement but do not, by themselves, uniquely diagnose the species (Linkem et al., 2011). The Sulu Forest Skink has records from Basilan (Uetz et al., 2026; Museum of Comparative Zoology, n.d.). The Sulu Forest Skink is reported from forests. Originally described as Sphenomorphus biparietalis in 1918, this species was subsequently transferred to Tytthoscincus. Its original holotype from Lapac Island in the Sulu Archipelago was reportedly destroyed during World War II; later identifications should recognize this type-material limitation (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

r.full: Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University (n.d.). Tytthoscincus biparietalis specimens R-26384 and R-20439. https://mczbase.mcz.harvard.edu/guid/MCZ:Herp:R-20439

records.p: The Philippine identification key describes Malayotyphlops ruber as lacking a pale collar behind the head and having fewer than 400 transverse scale rows between head and tail. Its dark dorsal stripe covers 15 scale rows across the anterior body, compared with 13 rows in the similar M. andyi (Weinell et al., 2019). The Red Worm Snake is documented on Samar (Uetz et al., 2026). The Red Worm Snake is reported from forests. Leviton and colleagues’ Philippine snake catalogue gives Samar Island as the historical type locality of Malayotyphlops ruber (originally Typhlops ruber), with holotype SMF 16616. Its treatment retains Samar distribution and identifies unresolved comparisons among Malayotyphlops populations; the type record is historical evidence, not a contemporary occupancy survey (Leviton et al., 2018). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine snake key separates Ramphotyphlops cumingii from its congeners by a third supralabial scale overlapping the ocular scale and by 24–28 longitudinal body-scale rows at midbody. The first character separates it from R. marxi, whereas the higher scale-row count separates it from the other species treated in the key (Weinell et al., 2019). The Cuming's Worm Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Norte, and Davao Oriental. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). The Cuming's Worm Snake is reported from forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Comparative diagnostic treatments have reported approximately 20 midbody scale rows for Ramphotyphlops olivaceus, versus 18 in Gerrhopilus hedraeus and 22 in R. suluensis. Such minute snakes often require careful scale counts and expert review because gross brown coloration is insufficient (Uetz et al., 2026). The Olive Worm Snake is documented on Basilan and Samar within Greater Mindanao. Mainland Mindanao has been suggested from aggregated records but is not confirmed in the specialist treatment; additional reports from the Sulu Archipelago are outside the PAIC (Leviton et al., 2018; GBIF.org, 2026). The Olive Worm Snake is reported from forests. The broad classification does not establish soil, litter, or other retreat sites at named Greater Mindanao localities. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A pitviper with a green to blue-green or darker grey-green ground colour, sometimes bearing irregular dark blotches or crossbars. A pale stripe or series of light spots may run along the outermost dorsal scale row, and the tail often contrasts in colour with the body. The second upper labial joins the scale bordering the facial pit (WildAlert, n.d.). Mindanao populations were treated cautiously as T. cf. flavomaculatus in Sanguila and colleagues’ regional survey (2016), so colour alone should not settle uncertain identifications. The Philippine Yellow-spotted Pitviper has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Yellow-spotted Pitviper is reported from forests. Documented prey categories include frogs, lizards and rodents; the species uses branches and other elevated vegetation for at least part of its activity (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

A shaggy greyish palm civet with a pale mask across the forehead, a small pale mark under each eye and pale spots beside the nostrils; the muzzle and ears are dark. The long, stocky body bears three rows of dark dorsal markings, while the lower legs and the long tail are dark rather than conspicuously ringed. These WildAlert external characters are useful for an initial palm-civet identification but are not a specimen-based key distinguishing all species in the Paradoxurus complex (WildAlert, n.d.). The Philippine Palm Civet is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range and Mount Apo (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Palm Civet is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Paradoxurus philippinensis (Jourdan, 1837). Its historical type locality is Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 recognizes P. philippinensis following taxonomic separation from the P. hermaphroditus complex. Older Philippine records under P. hermaphroditus require taxon-concept reconciliation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A measured Mt Kitanglad male specimen had a 35 mm forearm (Heaney et al., 2006). The Mindanao bat guide reports an adult forearm measurement of approximately 34 mm (elbow to wrist) (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Tailless Roundleaf Bat has historical reports from the Mount Kitanglad region of Mindanao. These older reports predate the current separation of Coelops hirsutus from related taxa (Heaney et al., 2006; Mammal Diversity Database, 2026; BatNames, 2026). The Philippine Tailless Roundleaf Bat is reported from forests, rivers, streams, caves and karst landscapes. The species was originally described as Chilophylla hirsuta (G. S. Miller, 1910). Its historical type locality is Alag River, opposite mouth of Egbert River, Mindoro, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The original name Phyllorhina antricola was based on a male bat from an abandoned mine near Paracale, Luzon. Peters (1861) reported an ear about 17 mm long and 15 mm wide, a transverse noseleaf with four cells in his terminology, a conspicuous frontal sac in the male, and a tail about 30 mm long, nearly twice the approximately 16.5-mm tibia length. The original male had a forearm about 39 mm long; the wing membranes attached at the tarsus, the fur had pale bases and cinnamon-brown tips, and the wing membranes were brown. These are measurements and observations of the historical type specimen, not verified identification limits for all Philippine populations. The Mammal Diversity Database now treats H. antricola as distinct from the older H. ater complex, but the reported forearm and pelage characters alone do not exclude other small roundleaf bats. Museum-grade comparison of noseleaf, cranial and dental characters is needed for difficult specimens; a flying bat or isolated forearm measurement is not enough. The Philippine Dusky Roundleaf Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Cotabato (Hollister, 1913). The Philippine Dusky Roundleaf Bat is reported from forests, caves, and karst areas. The species was originally described as Phyllorhina antricola (W. C. H. Peters, 1861). Its historical type locality is Paracali, Luzon I, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 recognizes this bat separately from the historical Hipposideros ater complex (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide reports an adult forearm measurement of approximately 47 mm (elbow to wrist) (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Large Mindanao Roundleaf Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Surigao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Large Mindanao Roundleaf Bat is reported from forests, caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Phyllorhina coronata (W. C. H. Peters, 1871). Its historical type locality is Mainit, Surigao del Norte Province, Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 42–48 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Forest Roundleaf Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Surigao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Heaney et al., 2006). The Philippine Forest Roundleaf Bat is reported from forests and has been documented roosting in caves, mines, culverts, hollow trees and spaces among tree buttresses (Heaney et al., 2006). Day roosts include caves, mines, culverts and tree hollows (Heaney et al., 2006). Compiled traits describe nocturnal aerial foraging on invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Phyllorhina obscura (W. C. H. Peters, 1861). Its historical type locality is "Paracali [= Paracali, Camarines Norte Province], Luzon," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 51–55 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Great Long-fingered Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Zamboanga del Norte, and North Cotabato. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Great Long-fingered Bat is reported from forests, caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio tristis (G. R. Waterhouse, 1845). Its historical type locality is "Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 39–45 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Sulawesian Free-tailed Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Sulawesian Free-tailed Bat is reported from forests, rivers and streams, and cultivated areas. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Nyctinomus sarasinorum (A. B. Meyer, 1899). Its historical type locality is "Batulappa, nördlich vom See von Tempe [= north of Lake Tempe], SW Central Celébes [= Sulawesi]," Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A large fruit bat with medium to pale-brown fur and face, and paler brown flight membranes interrupted by conspicuous white blotches, especially along the leading wing edge and near the tip. The IUCN account reports a forearm of 135–145 mm and contrasts it with the nearly black wings and face of the similar-sized Pteropus hypomelanus. The IUCN source spells the specific name leucopterus; this manuscript follows the feminine ending leucoptera used by the Mammal Diversity Database (Waldien & Duya, 2020, summarizing Heaney et al., 2010). Within Greater Mindanao, the White-winged Flying Fox has a documented distribution on Dinagat Island. Published range treatments place the species otherwise in the Luzon faunal region and do not establish a regular population on Mindanao mainland. The regional account follows Dinagat records reported under the spelling Desmalopex leucopterus, while retaining the checklist name Desmalopex leucoptera (Waldien & Duya, 2020; DENR-BMB, 2018). The White-winged Flying Fox is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Pteropus leucopterus (Temminck, 1853). Its historical type locality is "îles Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 notes the transfer from Pteropus to Desmalopex and the feminine adjectival ending leucoptera rather than historical leucopterus. Older literature under Pteropus must be reconciled before extracting records (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

r.short: Waldien & Duya, 2020, summarizing Heaney et al., 2010

records.p: The taxonomic revision treats this as a large Dyacopterus fruit bat: examined specimens had forearms exceeding approximately 90 mm and greatest cranial lengths exceeding approximately 40 mm, with palatal ridge counts also useful in distinguishing congeners. These were characters used in the original comparison, not standalone cutoffs for all populations (Helgen et al., 2007). The Philippine Large-headed Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Large-headed Fruit Bat is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Dyacopterus rickarti (K. M. Helgen, Kock, Gomez, & Ingle in K. M. Helgen, Kock, Gomez, Ingle, & M. H. Sinaga, 2007). Its historical type locality is "San Isidro (17°27'N, 120°37'E), Luzon (Abra Province), Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Males bear a more developed scented chest ruff than females. The cited mammal treatment reports forearm measurements around 76–91 mm, with a relatively robust build for a small Philippine fruit bat (Wilson & Mittermeier, 2019). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 76–90 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Greater Musky Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Greater Musky Fruit Bat is reported from forests, caves and karst landscapes. The species was originally described as Pachysoma (Ptenochirus) Jagorii (W. C. H. Peters, 1861). Its historical type locality is Daraga, Albay, Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A fruit bat with a dark grey head and muzzle, a conspicuous rusty-brown ruff around the neck and shoulders, and grey-brown to rusty body fur. Relative to typical Ptenochirus, P. wetmorei has an exceptionally reduced tail that may appear externally absent and a weak or inconspicuous groove on the inner face of the upper canine. It was once described under Megaerops because of its reduced tail, but phylogenetic comparisons support its placement in Ptenochirus. Reliable discrimination from similar fruit bats still requires careful dental and cranial comparison (Almeida, Simmons & Giannini, 2020). The Mindanao Fruit Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Kampalili, Mount Lumot, Mount Daguma, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Yangurin et al., 2025). The Mindanao Fruit Bat is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Megaerops wetmorei (E. H. Taylor, 1934). Its historical type locality is Cotabato near Tatayan, Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 places wetmorei in Ptenochirus, rather than the historical genus Megaerops, following Almeida and colleagues (2020). Earlier references may use Megaerops wetmorei (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 118–133 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Gray Flying Fox has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Gray Flying Fox is reported from forests and cultivated areas. Its cited trait compilation characterizes it as a fruit-eating, nocturnal, arboreal forager, but does not provide a region-specific comparison of forest and agricultural habitat use (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled traits describe fruit feeding, arboreal foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Pteropus speciosus (Andersen, 1908). Its historical type locality is "Malanipa Island, off [west coast of] Zamboanga," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 49–55 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Philippine Forest Horseshoe Bat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Matutum, Agusan del Norte, and South Cotabato. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney et al., 2006). The Philippine Forest Horseshoe Bat is reported from forests, settlements, and other disturbed areas. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus inops (Andersen, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Mt. Apo, at Jodaya, Mindanao, 4000 feet [= 1219 m]," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 43–44 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Big-eared Horseshoe Bat has been documented on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Big-eared Horseshoe Bat is reported from caves and karst landscapes. A comparative mammal-trait compilation lists a litter size of approximately one young for this bat (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus macrotis (B. H. Hodgson in E. Blyth, 1844). Its historical type locality is Nepal (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 68–73 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Large Rufous Horseshoe Bat is recorded on Leyte and Bohol. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013; GBIF.org, 2026). The Large Rufous Horseshoe Bat is reported from caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rhinolophus luctus Varietas rufa (Eydoux & P. Gervais, 1836). Its historical type locality is "Manille [= Manila]," Luzon, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Narrow-winged Pipistrelle was described under the name Pipistrellus stenopterus in a Southeast Asian comparative account. Its short fur is dark chocolate to reddish brown, with blackish ears and wing membranes, a heavy muzzle and rounded ears bearing a broad, forward-angled tragus. The fifth metacarpal is shorter than the fourth, producing characteristically narrow wings. The cited study reports adult forearm lengths of 37–42 mm (Leong et al., 2010). The Narrow-winged Pipistrelle has been recorded on Mindanao (Ingle et al., n.d.; ASM, 2026). The Narrow-winged Pipistrelle is reported from forests and habitats along rivers and streams. The species was originally described as Vesperugo stenopterus (Dobson, 1875). Its historical type locality is "Sarawak, Borneo," Malaysia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 records a transfer from Pipistrellus to Alionoctula following Zhukova and colleagues (2025). Earlier regional literature may therefore be indexed under the former genus (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

In the Field Museum guide to Mindanao bats, the Least Pipistrelle appears under the earlier name Pipistrellus tenuis, with an adult forearm range of 30–32 mm. It is currently placed in Alionoctula. Although generally smaller than the Javan Pipistrelle in that guide, the reported ranges meet at 32 mm, so forearm length is only a preliminary sorting character. Dental, skull and other diagnostic measurements should be checked before reporting a definitive identification, especially because older tenuis records may refer to differing taxonomic concepts (Ingle, Sedlock, & Heaney, n.d.; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Least Pipistrelle is documented from Mindanao (Ingle et al., n.d.; ASM, 2026). The Least Pipistrelle is reported from forests and waterways. The species was originally described as Vespertilio tenuis (Temminck, 1840). Its historical type locality is Sumatra, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 notes both the transfer from Pipistrellus to Alionoctula and a historical species delimitation that included A. murrayi. Older name-based records require specimen or taxonomic-concept confirmation before transfer (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Peters’s Pipistrelle has dark chocolate-brown, long woolly dorsal fur with paler tips that produce a frosted appearance. A recently examined specimen also showed broad rounded ears, a short blunt tragus, a small patch of pale fur near the hindlimb and anus, and a slightly projecting tail tip. Identification among similar pipistrelles may require dental or genetic comparison (Guo et al., 2026). The Peters's Pipistrelle has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area (GBIF.org, 2026). The Peters's Pipistrelle is reported from forests, settlements, and other disturbed areas. The species was originally described as Vesperugo petersi (A. B. Meyer, 1899). Its historical type locality is Minahassa, northern Sulawesi, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 33–35 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Hardwicke's Woolly Bat has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Hardwicke's Woolly Bat is reported from forests. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). A comparative mammal-trait compilation lists a litter size of approximately one young for this bat (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Vespertilio hardwickii (Horsfield, 1824). Its historical type locality is Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide reports an adult forearm measurement of approximately 35 mm (elbow to wrist) (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Clear-winged Woolly Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range and Mount Hilong-Hilong (GBIF.org, 2026). The Clear-winged Woolly Bat is reported from forests and shrublands. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio pellucidus (G. R. Waterhouse, 1845). Its historical type locality is Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 30–31 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Whitehead's Woolly Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range (GBIF.org, 2026). The Whitehead's Woolly Bat is reported from forests, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and cultivated areas. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Kerivoula Whiteheadi (O. Thomas, 1894). Its historical type locality is "Isabella, N.E. Luzon," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

In the 2025 taxonomic revision, the Philippine type series is unusually small within the Murina cyclotis group. The authors reported forearm lengths of 33.7 mm for the measured male and 35.8 mm for the measured female; the dorsal fur shows greyish-buff bases with reddish-brown tips. Measurements refer to these specimens, not a known species-wide range (Eger et al., 2025). The Alvarez's Tube-nosed Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Alvarez's Tube-nosed Bat is reported from forests, caves and karst landscapes. The taxonomic series includes postlactating females recorded in May on Mt. Hamiguitan and in August on Cebu. These are dated reproductive-condition observations and do not establish a fixed breeding season across the species (Eger et al., 2025). The species was originally described as Murina alvarezi (Eger, Sedlock, B. K. Lim, & Heaney, 2025). Its historical type locality is Cebu Province, Cebu Island (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Tubular nostrils project from the nose, and the ears are short and rounded with tapered, triangular tragi. Both reddish-brown and greyer pelage forms are described (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 36–39 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Field Museum Mindanao bat guide lists adult forearm length as 36–39 mm for Murina cyclotis (Ingle et al., Rapid Color Guide No. 49, v1.2). PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 9.3 g and forearm length 34.4 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Round-eared Tube-nosed Bat has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Magdiwata, Agusan del Norte, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Round-eared Tube-nosed Bat is reported from forests. The cited account describes maneuverable, low-level flight and roosting in sheltered foliage. Some observations come from mainland Southeast Asia rather than the Philippines (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). PanTHERIA compiles litter size 2.0 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Murina cyclotis (Dobson, 1872). Its historical type locality is Darjeeling, India (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: Described as the largest Murina in the 2025 Philippine revision. The back has three-coloured hairs with pale-grey bases, buff middle portions and reddish-brown tips, contrasting with a predominantly white throat and central belly. The proximal half of the tail membrane carries long pale-orange hairs, and long hairs cover the feet beyond the claws; the ear has a notch along its rear edge. Its teeth resemble those of M. cyclotis, but it is larger in body and skull dimensions, and genetic and cranial features support separation. Field appearance alone is not conclusive for an uncatalogued tube-nosed bat (Eger et al., 2025). The Hilong-hilong Tube-nosed Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hilong-Hilong and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Hilong-hilong Tube-nosed Bat is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Murina hilonghilong (Eger, Sedlock, B. K. Lim, & Heaney, 2025). Its historical type locality is Mount Hilong-Hilong Range, Surigao del Sur, Mindanao, at approximately 85 m elevation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Described in 2025, Murina hilonghilong is based on specimens from the Mount Hilong-Hilong Range in Surigao del Sur, including holotype FMNH 190118 from approximately 85 m elevation (Eger et al., 2025).

records.p: The 2025 diagnosis reports a forearm length of 30.8–33.4 mm in its examined specimens, tricolored dorsal fur with darker bases and lighter intermediate bands, and reduced hair coverage of the wing membranes compared with some related Philippine tube-nosed bats. The published measurements are sample-bounded, not universal identification limits (Eger et al., 2025). The Philippine Tube-nosed Bat has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kampalili, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Tube-nosed Bat is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Murina philippinensis (Eger, Sedlock, B. K. Lim, & Heaney, 2025). Its historical type locality is Cebu Province, Cebu Island (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The 2025 revision of Philippine Murina recognized M. philippinensis as separate from populations previously placed within the M. suilla complex (Eger et al., 2025).

records.p: The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 35–38 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Horsfield's Myotis has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park and Mount Hilong-Hilong (GBIF.org, 2026). The Horsfield's Myotis is reported from rivers and streams as well as caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio horsfieldii (Temminck, 1840). Its historical type locality is Mount Gede, Java, Indonesia (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 44–49 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Pallid Large-footed Myotis is recorded on Leyte, Bohol, and Mindanao. On Mindanao, records include Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Pallid Large-footed Myotis is reported from caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits include invertebrates and fish, with aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Vespertilio macrotarsus (G. R. Waterhouse, 1845). Its historical type locality is "Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Mindanao bat guide gives adult forearm length of 30–34 mm, measured from elbow to wrist (Ingle et al., n.d.). The Nepalese Whiskered Myotis has been documented on Mindanao, Dinagat, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Nepalese Whiskered Myotis is reported from caves and karst landscapes. Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, aerial foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). A comparative mammal-trait compilation lists a litter size of approximately one young for this bat (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Vespertilio muricola (J. E. Gray, 1847). Its historical type locality is Nepal (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The original species description highlighted its distinctive stiff, golden-toned dorsal hairs, although the density and apparent color of these hairs varies among individuals (Heaney & Morgan, 1982). The Dinagat Gymnure has been documented on Dinagat (GBIF.org, 2026; Heaney & Morgan, 1982). The Dinagat Gymnure is reported from forests. Compiled dietary traits include invertebrates and endothermic vertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal and crepuscular activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Podogymnura aureospinula (Heaney & G. S. Morgan, 1982). Its historical type locality is "Plaridel, Albor Municipality, Dinagat Island, Surigao del Norte Province, Republic of the Philippines." Interpreted by D. R. Frost and colleagues in 1991 as "10°12'N, 125°35'E." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The smallest recognized Podogymnura in the 2023 revision, with head-and-body length 137–152 mm, a short tail of 49–66 mm, and long, soft dark reddish-brown dorsal fur bearing fine golden-brown tips. Ears and feet are pale; the tail is grey-brown above and almost unpigmented below. It differs clearly in its soft coat and smaller size from the larger, bristly P. aureospinula; it also has subtler golden spotting than P. intermedia. External measurements overlap slightly with P. truei, so specimen-based cranial comparisons may be required (Balete et al., 2023). The Kitanglad Gymnure has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Kitanglad Gymnure is reported from forests. The species was originally described as Podogymnura truei minima (Sanborn, 1953). Its historical type locality is Mt. Kitanglad, Bukidnon Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines, 1600 m (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 separates P. minima from P. truei based on the 2023 taxonomic reassessment by Balete and colleagues. Historical P. truei records may mix these taxa (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A Field Museum Mindanao rapid color guide reports head-and-body length of 130–152 mm, tail length of 45–65 mm and hind-foot length of 31–37 mm. These are comparative field-guide measurements, not a complete diagnosis (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Mount Apo Gymnure has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo, Mount McKinley, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). Compiled dietary traits include invertebrates and endothermic vertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal and crepuscular activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Mount Apo Gymnure is reported from forests. Arthropods occurred in all 31 examined stomachs; earthworms in 55% (Heaney et al., 2006). The species was originally described as Podogymnura truei (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Mount Apo at 6,000 feet [= 1829 m] altitude, southern Mindanao, Philippine Islands." Interpreted by D. R. Frost and colleagues in 1991 as "6°59'N, 125°16'E." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The 2023 revision of Podogymnura recognizes P. minima as distinct from populations formerly assigned to P. truei (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 30.9 g and head–body length 109.5 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Mindanao Lowland Forest Mouse has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Daguma. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Lowland Forest Mouse is reported from forests and is described in compiled traits as a nocturnal ground-forager eating plant material and invertebrates (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include other plant material and invertebrates, with ground foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Rattus (Apomys) littoralis (Sanborn, 1952). Its historical type locality is "Bugasan, altitude 50 feet [= 15 m], Cotabato Province, Mindanao Island, Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A long, narrow snout and small eyes and ears form part of the published external diagnosis (Rowsey et al., 2022). Dense dark fur covers the body. The visibly haired tail tapers and is shorter than head-and-body length (Rowsey et al., 2022). The type-series comparison reports head-and-body lengths of 131–143 mm and a tail close to 74% of head-and-body length (Rowsey et al., 2022). The published comparison uses external proportions and cranial traits, not snout shape alone, to distinguish Baletemys from related Philippine shrew-mice (Rowsey et al., 2022). The Kampalili Shrew Mouse is documented from montane and mossy forests of Mount Kampalili in eastern Mindanao (Rowsey et al., 2022). On Mount Kampalili, three shrew-mice were collected in lower montane and mossy forest at 1,640–1,900 m. Moss-covered fallen logs, thick humus, epiphytes and dense understory vegetation characterized the study sites (Rowsey et al., 2022). Earthworms were used as bait in some original captures but are not confirmed as part of its diet (Rowsey et al., 2022). Baletemys was described as a separate genus in 2022 and is recognized in Mammal Diversity Database v2.5 (Rowsey et al., 2022; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The mammal database documents a description from lower montane forest of Mount Kampalili in Mindanao (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The species was originally described as Baletemys kampalili (Rowsey, M. R. M. Duya, Ibañez, Jansa, Rickart, & Heaney, 2022). Its historical type locality is lower montane forest of Mount Kampalili, Davao Oriental, Mindanao, at approximately 1,640 m elevation (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: A trapped individual from eastern Samar was distinguished from Rattus everetti by the tail being noticeably shorter than head-and-body length, together with relatively long, moderately broad hind feet (Fernandez et al., 2020). The Mindanao Forest Rat has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mindanao Forest Rat is reported from forests. Plant remains and small amounts of arthropod material were found in stomach samples from Mount Kitanglad; the compiled traits describe primarily ground-based, nocturnal foraging (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). All three examined Mt Kitanglad stomachs contained plant remains (Heaney et al., 2006). In three stomachs examined from Mt. Kitanglad, researchers recorded trace arthropod remains in all 3 specimens (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). EltonTraits summarizes the diet as other plant material (60%), seeds (20%), fruit (10%), invertebrates (10%), with ground foraging and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Bullimus bagobus (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is "Todaya, a Bagobo village at 4,000 feet [= 1219 m] altitude on Mount Apo, southern Mindanao [Island], Philippine Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat is a large, long-furred rodent with orangish-tawny upperparts mixed with black guard hairs and a paler orangish-brown underside. Its conspicuously hairy tail is tawny near the base, black through most of its length, and white at the tip. The published descriptive treatment places it between the larger Luzon C. schadenbergi and the smaller Ilin C. paulus in body size (Plazi TreatmentBank, n.d.). The Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat is recorded from Dinagat Island, particularly the forest landscapes of Dinagat Islands Province (Pitogo et al., 2026). The Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat is reported from forest and has compiled traits of nocturnal tree-foraging on fruit and other plant material (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit and other plant material, with arboreal foraging and nocturnal and crepuscular activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources identifies Dinagat hairy-tailed cloud rat Crateromys australis as Critically Endangered in its national threatened-species discussion (Department of Environment and Natural Resources, n.d.). The species was originally described as Crateromys australis (Musser, Heaney, & Rabor, 1985). Its historical type locality is "Balitbiton, Loreto Municipality, Dinagat Island, Surigao del Norte Province, Republic of the Philippines." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: A small, dark-furred shrew-mouse with short ears, small eyes and a comparatively short tail. Its dorsal coat has stiff, spiny hairs rather than the softer pelage of the sympatric Katanglad Shrew Mouse, C. suncoides. This coat-texture comparison is supported by the genus-level reappraisal of Giarla and colleagues (2025); external characters alone do not constitute a full specimen diagnosis. The Mindanao Shrew Mouse is recorded on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, and Mount Daguma. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mindanao Shrew Mouse is reported from montane habitats. In the Mount Kitanglad sample, stomachs contained both plants and arthropods; a wider trait compilation describes ground-based, mainly diurnal foraging (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). Small stomach samples contained both plant and arthropod remains (Heaney et al., 2006). Compiled traits describe a largely plant-based diet, ground foraging and daytime activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Crunomys melanius (O. Thomas, 1907). Its historical type locality is "North Central Mindanao [Island, Philippines]. 3000' [= 914 m]." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

Compared with the closely related L. bryophilus, its hind feet and tail are shorter and the underparts paler (Rickart et al., 2003). The shorter hind feet and shorter tail help separate it from L. bryophilus (Rickart et al., 2003). The Long-tailed Moss Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kalatungan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Long-tailed Moss Mouse is reported from forests. Plant material occurred in the Mount Kitanglad stomach samples, and compiled traits describe nocturnal foraging both on the ground and in vegetation (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). Stomach samples from Mount Kitanglad contained plant material (Heaney et al., 2006). Compiled traits indicate mainly plant-based feeding, some climbing while foraging, and nocturnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Limnomys sibuanus (Mearns, 1905). Its historical type locality is Mount Apo, 2012 m, Davao City Province, south-eastern Mindanao, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A stocky moss mouse with short, distinctly spiny dorsal fur, brownish-grey upperparts and a much paler greyish-white underside. Some examined specimens show a white midventral patch. Compared with T. apoensis, it has a shorter, harsher coat and paler feet and ears; its tail scales are comparatively large (Rickart et al., 2024). The Spiny Moss Mouse has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Matutum (GBIF.org, 2026). The Spiny Moss Mouse is reported from forests. EltonTraits characterizes it as a terrestrial forager on invertebrates, with activity spanning several parts of the day; species-level regional observations are needed to test those compiled patterns locally (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits describe invertebrate feeding, ground foraging and nocturnal, crepuscular and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Tarsomys echinatus (Musser & Heaney, 1992). Its historical type locality is Balisong, 823–1128 m, Tupi, Mount Matutum, South Cotabato Province, southern Mindanao Island, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

The original description characterizes Tarsomys orientalis as a relatively small earthworm mouse with dense, soft, dark brown to blackish dorsal fur, contrasting with the coarse, spiny pelage of T. echinatus. Diagnosis also considers the short tail, narrow hind feet and cranial characters, rather than pelage color alone (Rickart et al., 2024). The Kampalili Moss Mouse is known from forest habitats on Mount Kampalili in eastern Mindanao, with records from the Davao Oriental and Davao de Oro sides of the mountain (Rickart et al., 2024). On Mount Kampalili, study specimens came from lower montane forest at 1,470 m and old-growth mossy forest at 1,900 m, where the ground held deep leaf litter, fallen logs, ferns and moss beneath oak, conifer and laurel trees (Rickart et al., 2024). The species was originally described as Tarsomys orientalis (Rickart, Rowsey, Ibañez, Quidlat, Balete, & Heaney, 2024). Its historical type locality is "2 km S, 2 km W Kampalili peak, Maragusan Municipality, Compostela Valley Province [now Davao de Oro Province], Philippines, 1,900 m elevation, 7.2866°N, 126.2753°E" (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao rapid color guide lists head-and-body length of 77–102 mm, tail length 53–76 mm and hind-foot length 24–29 mm for this squirrel (Heaney et al., n.d.). The Philippine Pygmy Squirrel has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Basilan, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Pygmy Squirrel is reported from upland habitats. Trait data describe arboreal, diurnal foraging, and stomach samples from Mount Kitanglad contained plant and arthropod remains (Heaney et al., 2006; Wilman et al., 2014). In 2 stomachs examined from Mt. Kitanglad, researchers recorded plant material in 100% and arthropod remains in 100% (Heaney et al., 2006, Table 5). EltonTraits estimates a diet of other plant material (80%), invertebrates (20%), with arboreal foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). PanTHERIA compiles litter size 1.9 for comparison (Jones et al., 2009). The species was originally described as Sciurus concinnus (O. Thomas, 1888). Its historical type locality is Isabela, Basilan Island, Zamboanga Province, Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

A published species account in Wilson, Lacher and Mittermeier (2016) describes the Davao Squirrel as having buff-colored cheeks and a darkening stripe along the middle of the back from the nose to the tail base. Hairs in that dorsal stripe have dark bases and russet tips. The belly is apricot-buff, with a clear transition between the darker back, sides and paler underside. The central tail is described as russet, edged with black and then white, and the underside of the tail is less russet. The account reports male mean head-and-body length of 198 mm and mean tail length of 182 mm, without specifying the sample size in the accessible treatment. These are published external recognition characters, not a demonstrated unique diagnosis against other Philippine Sundasciurus. Sanborn (1952) named the taxon from Madaum in the Tagum area of Davao, and Wilson and Reeder (2005) noted possible conspecificity with S. mindanensis, S. philippinensis and S. samarensis. Until voucher-based comparative diagnosis and the species boundary are resolved, do not label an ordinary Mindanao squirrel as S. davensis solely from location, coloration or apparent size. The Davao Squirrel has been documented on Mindanao (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Davao Squirrel is reported from forests. Trait data describe chiefly daytime activity, a substantial fruit component in the diet and foraging that includes the ground; these traits are compiled rather than measurements from a specific Davao study (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Callosciurus davensis (Sanborn, 1952). Its historical type locality is "Madaum, 25 feet [8 m] altitude, Tagum Municipality, Davao Province, Mindanao Island, Philippines Islands." (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

In a historical review of Mindanao specimens treated as Sciurus cagsi, now included under Sundasciurus mindanensis, Meyer described a bushy tail mottled reddish brown, black and white above, brown beneath with a black stripe along each side, and white margins and tip. A reddish colour at the tail base was also emphasized. Meyer reported disagreement between Steere’s original description of S. mindanensis and the specimens he examined, especially in the colour of the feet and tail. These historical traits describe the material examined, not a validated identification key for every modern Mindanao squirrel (Meyer, 1896; American Society of Mammalogists, 2026). The Mindanao Squirrel has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mindanao Squirrel is reported from forests and cultivated areas. EltonTraits describes mainly daytime foraging and a diet of fruit, other plant matter and some invertebrates; the compilation does not determine how frequently the species uses either habitat in Greater Mindanao (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciurus Mindanensis (Steere, 1890). Its historical type locality is Mindanao I (Philippines) (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

records.p: The Mindanao rapid color guide gives head-and-body length of 174–210 mm, tail length of 130–205 mm and hind-foot length of 37–52 mm. Identification among squirrels still requires plumage and other traits (Heaney et al., n.d.). A Hijo Forest species profile describes dark-brown dorsal pelage with paler hair tips and grayish to light-brown underparts, while warning that pelage color varies geographically (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Tree Squirrel has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Bega Watershed, and Sultan Kudarat. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Tree Squirrel is reported from montane habitats. Its compiled ecological traits describe diurnal foraging and a diet comprising fruit, other plant material and a smaller invertebrate component (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciurus Philippinensis (G. R. Waterhouse, 1839). Its historical type locality is "Mindanado (= Mindanao I)," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).

PanTHERIA compiles adult mass 225.0 g and head–body length 210.0 mm for the historical species concept (Jones et al., 2009). The Samar Squirrel has records from Samar and Leyte. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Samar Squirrel is reported from forests and agricultural areas. Trait data describe daytime activity and feeding on fruit, other plant material and some invertebrates, but provide no habitat-use comparison between Samar and Leyte (Wilman et al., 2014). Compiled dietary traits include fruit, other plant material, and invertebrates, with ground foraging and diurnal activity (Wilman et al., 2014). The species was originally described as Sciurus Samarensis (Steere, 1890). Its historical type locality is "Samar and Leyte," Philippines (American Society of Mammalogists, 2026).
